Foreword In the Name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate.
All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, Who opens the doors of maʿrifah to whom He wills, and places within the hearts of His servants the light of His remembrance. Endless blessings and salutations be upon the Seal of the Prophets, Sayyidunā Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), the ocean of divine mercy, the intercessor of the Ummah, and upon his purified family, the Ahl al-Bayt, who are the lanterns of guidance, and upon his noble companions, inheritors of truth and carriers of light.
 It is with gratitude and spiritual contentment that I place these words as a humble foreword to this important work by Amin Patel, a devoted seeker, practitioner of rūḥāniyyāt, and a researcher who has demonstrated both discipline and adab in traversing the delicate paths of the unseen sciences. In an age where sacred knowledge is either neglected or mishandled, it is rare to encounter a work that balances transmission (naql) with realization (taḥqīq), and outward scholarship with inward refinement.
The Ḥizb al-Baḥr, as bestowed by the great Imām Abū al-Ḥasan alShādhilī (may Allāh be pleased with him), is not merely a litany. It is a living ocean, vast and immeasurable, containing within it secrets that have sustained awliyāʾ and protected seekers across generations. Its recitation has been a shield against calamities, both seen and unseen, and a means of drawing near to the Divine Presence. The one who approaches it with permission (idhn), sincerity, and spiritual discipline finds within it openings that cannot be described by pen alone.
 Our brother Amin Patel has not approached this work lightly. Having received idhn and fulfilled the zakāh (riyadah) of the Ḥizb through the silsilah of the Chishtī-Ṣābrī masters in India, he has demonstrated commitment not only to the words but to the responsibilities that

accompany them. This is essential, for the sciences of rūḥāniyyāt are not mere texts to be translated, but trusts (amānah) to be carried with humility and restraint.
 This present work, inspired by the towering legacy of Shāh Walī Allāh Dihlawī (may Allāh have mercy on him), revives a dimension of understanding that is urgently needed today. Shāh Walī Allāh was among those rare inheritors who combined outward mastery of the Sharīʿah with deep penetration into the inner sciences. His engagement with litanies such as Ḥizb al-Baḥr was not theoretical. It was lived, practiced, and tested in the crucible of spiritual struggle.
 We must also remember the luminous legacy of the Chishtī masters in the lands of Hind. From Khwāja Gharīb Nawāz Muʿīn al-Dīn Chishtī (may Allāh be pleased with him) to Sulṭān al-Mashāʾikh Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyāʾ (may Allāh have mercy on him), these giants of the path were not only beacons of love and compassion but also formidable protectors of the believers against unseen harms. They encountered the practitioners of siḥr and occult forces not with fear, but with the strength of tawḥīd and the light of dhikr, transforming hearts, dismantling oppression, and, by Allāh's permission, guiding many from darkness into Islām. Their path reminds us that rūḥāniyyāt is not escapism. It is responsibility, service, and vigilance.
Likewise, we pay homage to Imām al-Shādhilī (may Allāh be pleased with him), whose ocean continues to flow through the hearts of the awliyāʾ, and to Shāh Walī Allāh Dihlawī, whose insights bridged worlds and whose legacy continues to nourish seekers in every age.
 The translation and commentary you now hold is therefore not a casual effort. It is part of a necessary revival. For too long, such works have remained inaccessible, locked behind language barriers or misunderstood by those lacking proper grounding. Bringing this knowledge into clarity, with respect for its depth and conditions, is a service to the Ummah.

However, let it be understood: this path requires adab, guidance, and sincerity. Text alone is not enough. One must seek permission, align intention, and purify the heart. Without this, even the most sacred words may remain veiled.
 I pray that Allāh grants acceptance to this work, places barakah within its pages, and makes it a means of protection, illumination, and nearness for those who approach it rightly. May He bless Amin Patel for his efforts, increase him in sincerity and insight, and allow this contribution to stand among those works that serve both the outer and inner dimensions of this faith.
 And peace and blessings be upon our master Muḥammad, and upon his family and companions altogether.
With prayers and humility,
 Sayyid Hamza Jalalpuri
 Khādim of the Jalālpurī Chishtia Silsila

Introduction In presenting this English rendering of Shāh Walī's inspired commentary on the Ḥizb al-Baḥr of Imām Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī, I do so with a clear awareness of both the value and the limitations of the present work.
The original commentary, composed in Persian, reflects a deeply rooted intellectual and spiritual tradition that flourished in the Indian subcontinent during a period marked by considerable political and social upheaval. Shāh Walī's contribution stands as a testament to the continuity of Shādhilī spiritual insight within a broader Indo-Islamic scholarly milieu, where synthesis rather than fragmentation defined the transmission of sacred knowledge.
 This translation has not been undertaken from a critical edition of the original Persian text. Rather, it is based on an Urdu manuscript, itself a non-critical transmission, and one that unfortunately contains missing pages. These textual constraints have necessitated a degree of interpretive discretion, and while every effort has been made to preserve fidelity to the author's intent, this work should be approached as a provisional bridge rather than a definitive scholarly reconstruction. All errors are on my part as the compiler and translator and not to be attributed to the original author, whose scholarship was far above such errors.
 The impetus for this work is fundamentally one of khidma: an act of service to the spiritual masters, and to the most Holy One (peace and blessings be upon him and his noble family) through whom the Ḥizb alBaḥr was bestowed upon Imām al-Shādhilī (raḍiy Allāhu ʿanhu). At present, English-speaking readers have only limited access to the rich and layered commentarial tradition surrounding the Ḥizb al-Baḥr. While the translation of Sīdī Aḥmad Zarrūq's commentary by Sidi Khalid Williams has provided an important and commendable point of entry, the perspective of Shāh Walī, shaped by the intellectual and spiritual currents of the Indian subcontinent, remains largely inaccessible.

It is hoped that this translation contributes to expanding that horizon, offering an additional interpretive lens through which the Ḥizb may be approached, understood, and lived. Whereas Sīdī Zarrūq's commentary, rooted firmly within the Shādhilī tradition, emphasises tawḥīd and a deep exegesis of the text's meanings, Shāh Walī's (who was Naqshbandi) treatment extends the discourse further into the domain of rūḥāniyyāt, integrating spiritual cosmology and experiential dimensions alongside the metaphysical foundations of tawḥīd.
 On a personal note, this work is not detached from lived spiritual experience. Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, during my journeying in India, I was granted khusus idhn by the Chishtī-Ṣābrīs at the maqām of Shaykh ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq Rudawlī to undertake the zakāh of the Ḥizb alBaḥr. The prescribed conditions were subsequently completed during the lockdown period, while in a state of iḥrām during my time in the Ḥijāz, incidentally not far from the Red Sea. These experiences, though personal, form part of the inward context in which this translation was carried out, and not a theoretical excercise that currently plagues academia, particularly in sufi and Akbarian circles.
 Two years thereafter, during travels to India and was afforded the opportunity to pay homage at the final resting place1 and maqām of Shāh Walī in Delhi. That visit served not only as a moment of closure, but as a reaffirmation of the living continuity of the tradition to which this text belongs. Thereafter, I also revisited a muftī and my longstanding rūḥāniyyāt mentor in Gujarat who teaches at a dār al-ʿulūm, who, upon hearing that I had since completed over ten thousand recitals of the Ḥizb al-Baḥr (for sulook), verified and then pointed out that I had reached the rank of a spiritual healer in the rūḥāniyyāt world, and that the muwakkils of the Ḥizb al-Baḥr were awaiting my commands.
This translation is therefore offered with humility: as an initial step toward making Shāh Walī's insights accessible to a wider audience, and

❦ And subjugate for us every sea that is Thine, in earth and heaven, in dominion and sovereignty, the sea of this world and the sea of the next.
from the Ḥizb al-Baḥr
 ❦

Apology of the Urdu Translator (from the original Farsi manuscript)
 It is a matter of regret that no clean (ṣaḥīḥ) manuscript of this book was available, by which the text could have been corrected. People of refined taste (ahl-i dhawq) will surely feel the loss. The readers are therefore earnestly requested to overlook minor mistakes and to amend the errors that they encounter.

The Author's Opening In the Name of God, the All-Merciful, the All-Compassionate.
All praise is due to God, Lord of the Worlds, and prayer and salutations upon our master Muḥammad and upon his pure family and his chosen Companions.
Thereafter: this faqīr Walī Allāh declares that what follows are some words which descended into the heart by way of inspiration (ilhām) at a time of inspiration concerning Ḥizb al-Baḥr, that famous litany which descended into the heart of Ḥaḍrat Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his sacred soul) by way of ilhām, and to which the name Ḥawāmiʿ (the Comprehensive Things) has been given.2
 This treatise consists of an Introduction (muqaddimah), Purpose (maqṣad), and Conclusion (khātimah). The introduction is divided into subtle discussions (mabāḥith). Whoever has even a slight acquaintance with Ḥizb al-Baḥr will find that everything contained herein is plainly intelligible, and the words of the litany itself will become exceedingly easy to him.
 Editorial note: The Arabic ḥawāmiʿ is the plural of jāmiʿ ("that which gathers" or "the comprehensive"), and is the same word from which the noun "jamʿah" (a session or gathering) is derived. The author's choice of title is significant: it positions his commentary not as a paraphrase of the litany but as a comprehensive gathering of all the meanings and uses which the litany contains. Each of the twelve mabāḥith and twenty jamʿahs that follow is, in effect, one comprehensive gathering.
2

THE INTRODUCTION (Muqaddimah) First Discussion: On the Recognition of the Perfection of Divine Governance (tadbīr) It should be known that the causes of the acceptance of supplication are many, and Ḥizb al-Baḥr is a supplication whose acceptance has been witnessed innumerable times. The acceptance of supplications takes one of two principal forms, and within each form there are subdivisions which the gnostic must distinguish.3 First. That the supplication has, in itself, an inherent efficacy and an inherent suitability for being answered. Every supplication contains within it a quality which makes it apt to be received. As for what specifically pertains to perfection of original creation, of natural disposition, and of acquired character: such was the supplication of His Excellency Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his soul). When such a supplication is uttered, the inward power of the supplicant produces a hidden subtle effect (athar laṭīf) in the world.
Second. That the supplication corresponds (muwāfaqat) with some hidden Divine wisdom, in such a way that, at the precise moment when the supplication is offered, the Divine governance has already prepared the means for that need to be met. The supplication and the answer meet Editorial note: The doctrine that supplication has "two principal forms" (one residing in the inherent qualities of the supplication, the other in the correspondence between the petition and a pre-arranged divine wisdom) is the conceptual hinge of the entire Ḥawāmiʿ.
It allows Shāh Walī Allāh to maintain, simultaneously, two positions that the rationalists and the literalists tend to set against one another: that supplication has real causal efficacy in the world, and that nothing happens except by an antecedent decree. The reader who keeps this two-fold structure in mind will find that almost every later claim in the work, on planetary intelligences, on the binding of the divine names to natural forces, on the daʿwah malakiyyah, is a development of one or the other of these two forms.
3

at one appointed moment. As an example: a person becomes hungry on a journey, and just at that moment another traveller appears upon his way carrying provisions, and a meeting takes place. Apparently this is a coincidence; in reality it is the working of an exact divine governance.
Third. That all the affairs of the cosmos, from the highest of the heavens to the lowest depths of the earth, are settled by an unerring providence. To the limited human intellect much of what occurs appears as accidental or surprising; in reality every particular fits into a pattern of governance whose horizon is incomprehensibly vast.
Fourth. That when God Most High intends to bring some perfection of management into the realm of action, He causes that perfection to appear first in the higher world, for the higher world is the place where the originative forms of all earthly events are first impressed; and only after their settlement there do they descend into the lower world. The Sufis call this prior settlement "the design upon the Preserved Tablet";
the philosophers call it "the descent of the universal forms upon particular preparedness."
Fifth. That, in correspondence with this descent, the supplication of the perfect ones takes effect: their words are themselves of the same world from which the descent comes, and so the supplication and the descent meet without distortion. This is one secret of why the prayers of the great gnostics are answered in ways that astonish ordinary observers.
The recognition of the perfection of tadbīr is thus the first foundation upon which the science of Ḥizb al-Baḥr rests: for whoever does not believe that all things are settled by an exact providence cannot recognise that a single sentence of the litany, struck at the precisely appointed moment, can move oceans, restrain enemies, repel storms, and open ways.
Sixth. That the four elements (the four ʿanāṣir, fire, air, water, earth) and the seven planetary forces, together with the angels and jinn appointed over each of them, are all servants in this governance: each

obeys, each is at its station, each carries out its appointed effect. The recognition of this corps of secondary causes does not amount to belief in independent agents; rather, the gnostic sees them as the appointed limbs of a single Divine purpose.

Second Discussion: Concerning the Theophany (tajallī) which was the Qiblah of the Aspiration (himmah) of Shaykh Abū alḤasan al-Shādhilī When God Most High created the world by the perfection of His tadbīr, fashioning the heavens, the earth, and whatever is between them, He removed the darkness of pure non-existence by a certain theophany (tajallī) such that the entirety of the world was clothed in the garment of a luminous theophany. This theophany has stations and degrees, and the himmah of the perfect ʿārif is directed at one or another of these stations according to his preparedness.4 First. It is established (muqarrar) that fire kindles itself by its own self in a piece of wood, so that wood and fire become one. In the same way, the world was kindled by an eternal Light into being. Once this kindling occurred, the world flamed up with subsistence; and the perfection of every existent thing, the angels of the spheres, the planetary souls, and the souls of men, became, as it were, sparks taken from that single Fire.
Second. Within this theophany, certain stations are distinguishable.
The most exalted station is the theophany upon the Throne (al-tajallī ʿalā al-ʿarsh), beyond which the human intellect cannot pass; for this is the station of the Most Sacred Outpouring (al-fayḍ al-aqdas), the place of the originative inscription of all the realities. From this station the Light pours down upon the spheres, then upon the souls of the prophets and Editorial note: The metaphysics of tajallī here is unmistakably Akbarī, drawing upon the line that runs from Ibn ʿArabī through Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnawī and into the Indo-Persian tradition that Shāh Walī Allāh inherited. The remarkable feature of his treatment, however, is the operationalisation of the doctrine: tajallī is not merely a metaphysical postulate but a horizon to which the supplicant orients his himmah at the moment of recitation. The reader inclined to read the passage as mere theoretical decoration should note that everything which follows in the Maqṣad, all twenty jamʿahs, depends on the practical premise that the reciter can, at will, attune his orientation to a particular degree of theophany. The doctrine is here a tool, not an ornament.
4

saints, then upon the planetary intelligences, and so descends through the orders of being.
Third. Below this is the theophany upon the soul of the Perfect Man (al-tajallī ʿalā nafs al-insān al-kāmil), in which the gnostic receives in his own soul a reflection of what the Throne has received from the Source.
This is the station from which the saint draws the efficacy of his words;
and his words then carry the imprint of that station to the world below.
Fourth. Further below is the theophany upon the elemental world (ʿālam al-ʿunṣur), where the four elements receive into themselves the qualities sent down through the planetary intelligences. The perfect ʿārif is aware of this descent; the ordinary man receives its effects without recognising their cause.
Fifth. The qiblah of the aspiration of His Excellency Shaykh Abū alḤasan al-Shādhilī was directed precisely toward the highest of these, the theophany upon the Throne. His himmah did not stop at the planetary order, did not stop at the order of the angels of the spheres, but ascended to the seat of the Most Sacred Outpouring itself. From this seat his supplication drew its efficacy. Therefore, when his litany is recited, it is recited not as a petition that ascends from below, but as a participation in a Light that has already descended from above.
Sixth. It is therefore necessary for whoever would recite this litany with effect to direct his himmah, as far as he is able, toward that same horizon: not toward this or that secondary cause, not toward the apparent enemy or apparent need, but toward the Source from which both the cause and its removal proceed. The greater this orientation, the greater the effect.
Seventh. It must be added that the theophany is single in essence yet multiple in respect of those who receive it. Each receiver receives according to his own preparedness (istiʿdād): the spheres according to their natures, the angels according to theirs, men according to theirs. The

Shaykh's himmah was perfected to the degree that it received from the very source, and therefore his words, when transmitted to others, retain something of that originating power.
Eighth. Whoever recites the litany while inwardly imitating the Shaykh's orientation participates in his theophany by reflection. He does not ascend by his own merit; he ascends by attaching himself, in heart and intent, to one whose ascent has already been confirmed. This is one secret of the meaning of "the saints are the inheritors of the prophets."

Third Discussion: An Explanatory Note on the Symbols (rumūz) found in the Description of the Divine Talisman (ṭilism ilāhī) Conformity with the time of the appearance of the need is necessary;
for so long as the need has not appeared, the supplication is not engaged with it, and the heart cannot be present in the manner required. In this connection comes the question of the Divine Talisman (ṭilism ilāhī), by which is meant the order in which the Divine Names are bound to the natural and elemental forces of the cosmos, so that those forces obey them.5 First. By "talisman" is not meant a magical figure inscribed on a piece of metal, but the very binding-thread by which the Divine Will fastens the names of the higher world to the bodies of the lower world.
Whenever a creature is brought into being, a thread of correspondence runs from a particular Name of God, through a particular planetary intelligence, through a particular angelic functionary, into the matter of that creature.
Second. The people of the speaking soul (ahl-i nafs nāṭiqah) sometimes perceive these threads. To such-and-such a need such-andsuch a Name is bound; to such-and-such a planetary force such-and-such a quality is married. This perception is not granted to all in equal measure:
every gnostic perceives a portion in proportion to his preparedness (istiʿdād).
Editorial note: The word ṭilism (whence the English "talisman") will alarm the reader trained to associate it with the magical practices that orthodoxy has, with reason, condemned. Shāh Walī Allāh's usage is precise and quite distinct: the ṭilism in his sense is a metaphysical structure, not a craft. He intends the same reality that Ibn ʿArabī terms al-rabṭ al-ilāhī (the divine binding) and that the Mujaddidī line speaks of as taʿalluq alasmāʾ bi-l-makhlūqāt (the relation of the Names to creatures). The point of his usage of the older word is, I think, deliberately provocative: he is reclaiming a vocabulary that the people of folk-magic have stolen, and returning it to its rightful metaphysical context.
The reader who finds the word jarring may simply substitute "divine binding" wherever it appears.
5

Third. There is, however, a further fact: that the Divine Will may at any moment cut a particular thread and re-bind it elsewhere. Therefore the perceptions of the gnostic, however accurate at one moment, must be re-checked at the next; the saint who would supplicate by way of the bindings must be present, not relying upon a previous unveiling.
Fourth. The Shaykh, having attained the perfection of the highest Outpouring, perceived these bindings as a man perceives the limbs of his own body. He was therefore able to use the Names within the litany according to the precise binding required by the moment. Where another might say a Name in approximation, the Shaykh utters it with knowledge of the very thread upon which heaven and earth turn at that instant, and the answer follows as a consequence of an exact correspondence.
Fifth. Below the station of the highest tajallī are the planetary forces (qawā sayyārah), Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, each of which has been allotted a measure of dispositional influence in the formation of the bodies of this world. The Shaykh used to direct his himmah upward through these orders, finding each Name united with a particular force, and through that union returning to the originating Light.
Sixth. To recite Ḥizb al-Baḥr while ignorant of these bindings is permissible and beneficial; the simple believer who recites it benefits according to his sincerity. To recite it with awareness of them is to participate in the work of the gnostic himself. The Shaykh's intention was that even the unlettered should benefit, while the gnostic should benefit in proportion to his knowledge.

Fourth Discussion: That Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī had a Share in the Distribution of the Divine Mercy (raḥmah ilāhiyyah) Among the secrets of this litany, and the speech of God which follows in some of its verses, is this: it should be known that, in the way of the wayfarers and Sufis, by aspiration (himmah) is meant a movement of the soul which, when it is engaged perfectly upon any object, becomes a true cause of the fulfilment of that object. There appears, by the kindness of God, in the heart of the perfect gnostic a certain power of disposal (taṣarruf) by which he is given a portion of the distribution of the Divine mercy.6 First. It is in accordance with this principle that one says: God has made certain saints "hands of mercy" upon the earth, through them are sent rains and provisions, by their himmah are turned away calamities, and to their supplications are tied the loosing of difficulties. Such was Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī. His share in the distribution of mercy was so great that, during his lifetime and afterwards, calamities were turned away by his himmah and the himmah of his gnostic companions.
Second. This distributive function does not belong to him originally, but only by way of mediation: he is the channel and not the source. He himself emphasised this constantly, lest his disciples imagine that the saint creates anything. The saint is rather a polished mirror: when the Editorial note: The doctrine of saintly taṣarruf is among the most sensitive in this work, and is the doctrine most likely to provoke objection from the reader formed in a strictly purist theology. Shāh Walī Allāh is careful, here as elsewhere, to thread the needle: he affirms the reality of the saint's share in the distribution of mercy while emphasising that the saint is the channel and not the source. The position is a subtle one, and requires the reader to hold two thoughts simultaneously: that nothing acts but God, and that God has appointed certain of His servants to act on His behalf. Whoever drops the second thought falls into a deistic shrinkage of the divine economy; whoever drops the first falls into the very shirk that the doctrine is structured to avoid. The litany itself, recited in the spirit of this discussion, is a daily training in holding the two thoughts together.
6

Light strikes it, the place where the Light is reflected is illumined; but the Light belongs to the Sun.
Third. When the himmah of such a saint is engaged in supplication, the Light strikes through him into the world below; and what people see as the saint's miracle is in truth the ray of God's own mercy passing through a perfectly cleansed surface. To deny this is to deny the office of saintship as God has appointed it; to over-believe it is to fall into the error of associating partners. The middle position is the position of the people of the path.
Fourth. This share of mercy may be transmitted: the saint's followers, by recitation of his litanies and by attachment to his way, are themselves brought beneath the same channel. Hence the recitation of Ḥizb al-Baḥr by one who follows the Shādhilī way (or by anyone who reveres its author and has confidence in it) brings him beneath that channel, and the same mercy descends upon him by the inheritance of the Shaykh's intent. There is in this neither shirk nor exaggeration, only the fact of the appointed channel.

Fifth Discussion: On the Description of the Universal Faculty (mukmīl-i kulliyyah) The aspiring soul, by means of its recitation, derives benefit from the souls of the prophets and the saints, of whose dispensation the Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his soul) is one. By means of the litany, a power is imparted from those souls into the heart and limbs of the reciter, not by way of incarnation or transmission of essence, but by way of correspondence and resonance, as one tuned string answers another.7 First. The Universal Faculty (mukmīl-i kulliyyah, lit. "that which completes the whole") is the name given by some Sufis to the allcomprehending power of the perfected human reality (al-ḥaqīqah alMuḥammadiyyah), through which every individual capacity is brought to its perfection.
Second. By means of this Faculty the prayers of the saints are connected with the prayer of the Prophet (peace be upon him), and the prayer of every reciter who is in the chain is connected with the prayers of the saints. Thus the chain of efficacy descends from the Source through the Prophet, through the inheriting saint, through the litany, into the heart of the present reciter, and ascends again, bearing his need, by the same chain.
Third. The five conditions of recitation enumerated by Shaykh Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mursī (the great khalīfah of Imām al-Shādhilī), namely sincere intention, lawful livelihood, ritual purity in body and clothing, Editorial note: The image of the tuned string is mine, not the original's; the original speaks more abstractly of muwāfaqat (correspondence). I have substituted the metaphor because it captures, with a precision the abstract noun lacks, the mechanism the author is describing: not transmission of substance, not incarnation, not magical contagion, but the resonance by which a properly attuned receiver picks up a wave that already exists in the medium. In the original Persian, Shāh Walī Allāh's own preferred metaphor is the mirror;
both metaphors say the same thing, that the saint is not himself the cause but the receiver and re-transmitter of a Light that has its source elsewhere.
7

knowledge of what one is reading, and observance of the appointed times, are all contained within this principle of the Universal Faculty. Each condition opens an aperture in the heart for the Light of the chain to descend; and where any condition is missing, that Light is dimmed by that much.
Fourth. It is a duty upon the reciter, at the very moment of supplication, to bring before his heart's eye the figure of the Shaykh, and by means of that figure, the figure of the Prophet, and by means of the Prophet, the Presence of God Most High; and from that Presence let his need return back through the same chain into the world of secondary causes. This is what is meant by reciting with presence (ḥuḍūr); without it, the recitation is but a word upon the tongue.
Fifth. The presence of mind which the masters require is not a mere absence of distraction; it is a positive orientation of the heart toward the chain. Many people sit silent and call themselves present; in truth their hearts are merely empty, not directed. The fifth condition therefore is the most subtle: it asks of the reciter not silence but vigilance.
Sixth. Whoever cannot fulfil all five conditions should at least fulfil what he can. The mercy of God does not deny the reciter his portion merely because of his weakness in the conditions; only it gives him the portion that corresponds to his fulfilment. The reciter is therefore to begin where he is, with the determination to grow into the conditions over time.
Seventh. It is reported among the masters that the Shaykh himself used to say: "My recitation of the litany is not the recitation of one supplicant; it is the recitation of the chain." By this he meant that, at the moment of his recitation, he felt himself a member in a body whose head was the Prophet (peace be upon him); and the body of the litany ran through him into the world. This is the reality of the Universal Faculty in operation.

Eighth. The conclusion is this: that the litany is not a property; it is a doorway. Whoever enters by it enters into the company of those who have entered before him; whoever recites it sincerely is a guest at a table that has been set by another. To be ungrateful at this table is to be expelled from it; to be grateful is to be invited to remain.
Ninth. The reciter, having understood this, recites with both humility and confidence: humility because the litany is not his, confidence because the chain has been opened to him. He is neither proud nor despairing; he is a guest who knows the host.

Sixth Discussion: On the Cause for which the Tyrannical Governance (tadbīr-i ẓālim) Manifests If the Divine governance is, as has been established, perfect, without slip, without oversight, without injustice, then how is it that we observe in the world manifest tyranny, oppressive rulers, the prevalence of the wicked over the just, the affliction of the righteous, and the success of the corrupt? This question troubles the simple believer, and the gnostic too has his share in turning it over.8 First. It must be known that the appearance of tyranny in the world is the appearance of tadbīr in the manner of trial (tadbīr-i ibtilāʾ), and not in the manner of corruption of the original ordering. God Most High has appointed both the gentle face (tadbīr-i jamālī) and the severe face (tadbīri jalālī) of His governance; and the latter manifests through the agency of those whose souls are darkened, who are made instruments of trial for the souls of the upright.
Second. The signs by which the believer recognises the tyrannical aspect are several: a darkness pervades the affair, a heaviness upon the chest of those caught in it, a contraction of provision, a closing of doors, the springing-up of false witnesses, the ascendance of the corrupt over the upright, and a general veiling of the face of mercy.
Third. In such a state the heart of the perfect ʿārif feels a peculiar impulse: a desire to repel by means of supplication that which has come Editorial note: Shāh Walī Allāh's framing of the problem of evil here is worth pausing over. He does not mount a theodicy in the philosophical sense, that is, he does not argue that God permits evil because of some greater good that depends upon it. His move is rather practical: he reframes the apparent injustice as tadbīr-i ibtilāʾ, the governance of trial, and invites the believer to participate in its undoing through the litany. The philosophical reader may find this evasive; the practical reader will find it liberating. The author seems to be saying: I will not solve for you the metaphysical puzzle of why the wicked prosper. I will give you, instead, an instrument by which their prospering can, by the leave of God, be ended. The reader who is capable of bearing both the unsolved puzzle and the working instrument is the reader for whom this book is written.
8

down by way of trial. This impulse is not a complaint; it is a petition. The gnostic does not say "why has this been sent"; he says "please remove what has been sent." The first is rebellion; the second is worship.
Fourth. It is for this reason that prophets and saints have always been provided with litanies of repulsion: the prayer of Ibrāhīm against Nimrūd, the prayer of Mūsā against Firʿawn, the prayer of Sulaymān against the rebellious jinn and demons, the prayer of ʿĪsā against Iblīs, and the prayer of Muḥammad (peace and blessings of God upon them all) against the unbelievers and tyrants of his age. The litanies of the saints follow this same pattern. Ḥizb al-Baḥr is itself, in one of its principal aspects, a litany of repulsion.
Fifth. The recitation of such a litany at the time of trial is not a contradiction of tadbīr; it is itself part of tadbīr. For God has decreed that the trial should come, and has also decreed that the supplication shall lift it; the two are linked in a single arc, and the believer's recitation is the bowstring upon which both the descent of the trial and the descent of relief are strung. To recite it, then, is to act according to the wisdom of providence, not against it.

Seventh Discussion: On the Sequence of the Jinn (silsilah-i jinniyān) Connected with the previous discussion is the matter of the chain of the jinn, that is, the order in which jinnī beings exert influence within the world of generation, and the manner in which the perfect ʿārif handles their influence.9 First. It descended, by way of inspiration, into the heart of Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his soul) that there is a Universal Faculty by means of which every science is unveiled, and the precise way in which the descents of the higher faculties bind themselves to the elemental bodies of the world is made plain. The world is, as it were, layered: above are the planetary spheres and their angelic intelligences; below them are the four elements; and intermediate between them are the jinn, who, being formed of fire and air, possess subtle bodies capable of acting upon the elemental world below and of receiving impressions from the spheres above.
Second. From this followed the distinction of Quranic sciences from the analogies (qiyās) of the philosophers and from the disposition of the natural ʿulamāʾ. The Shaykh's followers, by way of transmission from him, used to say in their journeys: when the chain of the jinn rose against them, by means of the wind upon the sea, the fire of fevers, the
 Editorial note: The reader formed in the modern naturalistic worldview will find this discussion the most foreign in the work. I will not argue here for the existence of the jinn, the Quran is unambiguous about it, and Shāh Walī Allāh writes in a tradition for which their existence is not a matter of speculation but of received fact. What is worth noting, however, is the precision of the author's treatment: he is not invoking the jinn as a generic explanation for whatever in the world he cannot otherwise account for. He has a structural view: the jinn occupy a determinate position in the cosmic order (between the planetary intelligences above and the elemental forces below), and their influence is therefore predictable in its broad outlines. The reader sceptical of the existence of the jinn may, if he wishes, read the chapter as a phenomenology of the unseen forces that act upon the human soul, and will lose nothing essential by doing so.
9

whisperings of suspicion, or the open assault of unseen forces, they would recite the litany; and the chain would loosen, and the affair would pass.
Third. It is reported (and the Shaykh himself referred to this) that he once boarded a ship in the company of his disciples, intending the pilgrimage. They reached the open sea, and a contrary wind arose; the sailors gave up hope. The Shaykh said: "Be still; recite this with me."
And they recited the litany. By the blessing of God, the wind turned, the ship was righted, and they reached safety. Many such accounts have been transmitted.
Fourth. There is a further account: the ship was once approached by a contrary vessel manned by Christian pirates, and the Shaykh's companions were afraid. The Shaykh recited; and a wind arose from the contrary direction so strong that the pirate vessel was driven backward, and the Shaykh's company arrived safely in their port. When the captain of the pirate vessel later met the Shaykh in Cairo, he became a Muslim, having seen, with his own eyes, the litany become wind, and the wind become a wall.
Fifth. The reciter who knows that the wind, the wave, the fever, and the whispering each have a chain reaching upward through jinnī influence to the planetary forces and beyond, and that the litany, recited from the heart of an ʿārif, descends through the same orders to break that chain, will recite with the kind of awareness that gives the words their full effect.
Sixth. The Shaykh would, on certain occasions, name particular jinnī forces and command them by the Names contained in the litany; but he would warn his disciples not to attempt this without firm rooting in knowledge and sincerity, lest the very act be turned against the reciter.
The simple believer is to recite the litany whole, with confidence, and to leave the unveiling of the chain to whom God wills to unveil it for.

Eighth Discussion: Concerning the Varieties of the Apprehension of Meanings (fahm al-maʿānī) which are Particular to the Book of God and the Sunnah of the Messenger of God It is plain at the outermost level that meanings are extracted from the inner recesses (buṭūn) of the noble Quran. There are sciences of the Book of God which are deposited in many of the elevated phrases of that Book, sciences whose ordinary meanings (mafhūm and manṭūq) are accessible to those who know the language; but in addition there are subtleties (laṭāʾif) and meanings which descend, by way of taste and unveiling, only into the hearts of the people of God.10 First. The form of these descended meanings is varied. Sometimes the gnostic is reading a verse and a meaning suddenly stands forth which is in some respect different from, and yet not contrary to, the apparent meaning, it is rather a deeper layer.
Second. Sometimes a verse, while being recited, becomes the occasion for an unveiling concerning the reciter's own state. He was recited yesterday into one understanding; he is recited today into another.
The text has not changed; the reciter has descended into a deeper layer of it.
 Editorial note: This is the chapter that, more than any other in the work, marks Shāh Walī Allāh's place in the long argument over the legitimacy of inner (bāṭinī) interpretation of the Quran. His position is the classical Sufi mediating one: the inner meaning never abrogates the outer, but discloses a layer that sits beside it. The crucial test, in this tradition, is non-contradiction; an inner reading that contradicts the outward sense is not an inner reading at all but a heresy. The author has internalised this discipline so thoroughly that he never feels the need to state it explicitly; the reader formed in a different tradition should keep it in mind throughout, lest he confuse the author's allusive readings of Quranic verses with the kind of free-association that some have called "spiritual" but which the Sufi tradition properly classifies as ḥaẓẓ al-nafs (the fancy of the lower soul).
10

Third. Sometimes the verse, which in its outward sense referred to a past prophetic event, is found in the recitation to refer also to a present situation of the gnostic himself: the same words become a sword against his own enemies, a balm upon his own wounds, a guidance for his own perplexity.
Fourth. This kind of apprehension is what the people of the path call ishārah (allusion). It does not abrogate the outward (ẓāhir) sense; it discloses an inward (bāṭin) sense which sits beside it. The Shaykhs have always insisted upon this: that the inward and the outward are not contraries but companions; whoever rejects the inward forfeits the depth, and whoever rejects the outward forfeits the foundation.
Fifth. Examples are given by the gnostics: the verse "Yaʿlamu khāʾinata al-aʿyun" ("He knows the treachery of the eyes," Q 40:19), outwardly refers to God's knowledge of secret betrayal; inwardly to the wandering of the heart's eye toward what is other than God. "Falammā tajallā Rabbu-hu li-l-jabal" ("And when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain," Q 7:143), outwardly refers to Sinai; inwardly, to the manifestation of God upon the mountain of the human ego, which crumbles when it is touched by Him.
Sixth. Ḥizb al-Baḥr is composed almost entirely of Quranic verses and prophetic phrases, and that what makes it a litany rather than merely a recitation is precisely that, in the heart of the Shaykh, each verse was inwardly oriented toward a particular need. To recite the litany while only attending to the outward meaning is to cut off half its blessing; to recite it while attending also to the inward meaning is to receive the full descent.
Seventh. Concerning fāl (the augury or seeking-of-direction by recitation): the Sufis hold that, when the heart is sincere and the recitation is pure, the verses themselves will sometimes incline toward a particular meaning that becomes a guidance for the present moment, and this is to be received with gratitude, not with any claim. It is not to be sought for
trifles, nor used to coerce God's wisdom, but it does occur, and the Shaykh's litany is one of the channels by which it occurs.

Ninth Discussion: On the Meanings of the Disconnected Letters of the Mighty Quran (al-muqaṭṭaʿāt) It is well known that certain sūrahs of the noble Quran open with disconnected letters, Alif Lām Mīm, Yā Sīn, Ḥā Mīm, Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād, and the like. The mufassirūn have differed in their opinions concerning their meaning; the people of unveiling and the gnostics have, however, indicated some particularly subtle meanings concerning them, and this is one of the reasons why the litany of the Shaykh contains them.11 First. The principle, briefly, is this: every letter in the Arabic alphabet has been allotted a hidden correspondence with a special meaning in the unseen, letters of light, letters of fire, letters of air, letters of water, and letters of earth, in the technical reckoning. From this correspondence comes the science of the properties of letters (khawāṣṣ al-ḥurūf), which is one of the branches of the science of the unseen.
Second. The disconnected letters at the openings of the sūrahs concentrate within them the comprehensive meanings of those sūrahs in the manner of a coded inscription, of which the key is held by God and given out, in measure, to those whom He wills. By means of these letters the unveiled gnostic is given access to that storehouse.
Third. It is for this reason that the recitation of these letters with presence of heart bears a peculiar effect upon the soul, different from the effect of the verses that follow them. The reciter often experiences, at Editorial note: The science of the disconnected letters and, more broadly, the science of the properties of letters (khawāṣṣ al-ḥurūf or ʿilm al-ḥurūf) is among the most contested in the Islamic intellectual tradition. The literalists treat it as a deviation; the gnostics treat it as a major branch of the science of the unseen; the philosophers, when they treat it at all, classify it among the conjectural sciences. Shāh Walī Allāh's treatment here is restrained: he affirms that the letters carry meaning, but cautions repeatedly against attempting to operate the science. The implicit advice, which I take to be the practical wisdom of the chapter, is this: recite what the masters have given you in the order they have given it, and do not innovate. The litany itself is the safe form of the science of letters; everything beyond it is the property of those who have been authorised, and is dangerous in untrained hands.
11

their utterance, a contraction or expansion, an opening of a door, or a sudden illumination upon some affair.
Fourth. The Shaykh of the path, accustomed to the effect, used to lean upon them at moments of difficulty, knowing that beneath the apparent silence of the unintelligible letters there sits a Speech which sustains heaven and earth. The litany Ḥizb al-Baḥr makes deliberate use of certain of these letters: "Yā Sīn", "Ḥā Mīm" (repeated seven times), "Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād", "Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf", drawing upon the cumulative power of the inscriptions.
Fifth. The simple reciter receives a portion of this power by virtue of his recitation; the gnostic receives it consciously. It is to be remembered that the science of the letters is not to be played with: it is a serious branch of the unseen sciences, the misuse of which leads to error and ruin. The way of the litany is the safe way: to take what the perfect Shaykh has assembled, and to recite it with confidence in his ordering, leaving the science behind it to those whom God has appointed for that science.

Tenth Discussion: A Brief Indication concerning the Reality of the Angelic Invitation (daʿwat malakiyyah) and its Conditions Here a delicate matter is to be touched upon, the reality of what is technically called "the angelic invocation" or "the angelic invitation"
(daʿwat malakiyyah), and the conditions which the people of this knowledge have laid down concerning it.12 First. By daʿwat malakiyyah is meant a manner of invocation in which the reciter, in the act of supplication, deliberately addresses (by leave of God) those particular angelic intelligences which are appointed over the matter at hand, that is, his prayer ascends not only to God in general but, on its way, passes through and is accompanied by the angelic functionaries who carry petitions and bring back answers.
Second. This is the principle of Ḥizb al-Baḥr in its fullest form: that it is a daʿwah, a calling, in which Names of God, Quranic verses, and (by implication) the angelic chains are all engaged together at the moment of recitation. The reciter does not thereby take an angel as an object of worship; he takes the angel as a recognised servant in the body of governance.
Third. The conditions laid down by the masters for the safe and effective practice of such daʿwah are, in summary, the following: (1) the place of recitation should be clean and pure; (2) the body, clothing, and breath of the reciter should be in a state of purity; (3) the food eaten Editorial note: The technical term daʿwat malakiyyah is among those which a careless reader could easily misconstrue. It does not mean prayer to the angels; the Sufi tradition is unanimous that worship and supplication directed to anyone other than God are forms of shirk. The term means rather that the angels are recognised as appointed servants of the Divine Will and are addressed in their official capacity, in the same way that one might address the post-master not because the post-master is the source of the letter but because the letter has been entrusted to him for delivery. The litany itself, in this aspect, is a daʿwah in which the names of God are invoked, the prophets are mentioned by name, and the angelic functionaries are recognised, but the petition itself is directed solely to God. The reader should keep this distinction firmly in mind as he reads.
12

should be lawful; (4) the appointed times, usually the latter portion of the night, or the times between the dawn-prayer and sunrise, or in the late afternoon, should be observed; (5) the reciter should be free of rancour against any creature at the moment of recitation; (6) the heart should be attached to the Source and not to the secondary cause; (7) the number of repetitions and the order of the names and verses should be observed exactly as transmitted from the Shaykh; and (8) the recitation should be accompanied by sincere thankfulness for previous answers.
Fourth. Of these eight conditions, some are essential and some are auxiliary; whoever cannot meet all should at least meet the first four, and recite with confidence in the Shaykh's intent. The litany has, by the testimony of generations, brought relief to those who recite it under conditions far less than perfect; but the more the conditions are met, the more freely the descent flows.
Fifth. In the body of the litany, the reciter will find, at certain places, indications of an upward direction (toward the Throne) and at certain places indications of a downward direction (toward the elemental bodies).
The gnostic Shaykh used to vary the inclination of the heart accordingly:
when the litany ascends, the heart is directed up; when it descends, the heart is directed down. In this way the recitation traces, within the human heart, the very pattern by which the Divine governance moves through the world.
Sixth. To know this is to recite with knowledge; to do it is to recite with effect. The unlettered reciter who recites without this knowledge nevertheless receives a benefit, by virtue of his sincerity; but the gnostic reciter who knows and does is the one whom the angels themselves accompany.

Eleventh Discussion: On Certain Special Properties (khawāṣṣ) of Ḥizb al-Baḥr which this Faqīr has Discovered through the Light of Divine Aid (tawfīq nūr) Having stated the manner of its use and an explanation of its outpouring, this faqīr now mentions some particular properties of certain phrases of the litany which have come to be known through the kindness of God in the form of a special grace. The reciter who is in need of any of these effects should approach the corresponding phrase with attention, repeat it the indicated number of times, and watch with sincerity for the result.13 First. If a person is in need of a particular thing, and there is some difficulty preventing the achievement of it, let him address that thing through the litany itself. He should consider before him a form similar to the form of the need, and recite the phrase he has chosen seven times in his concentration upon that form, and then add a special invocation. The phrase should be repeated three or seven or twelve times, these being the numbers most frequently used in this practice, for it has been observed that the recitation of the phrase a particular number of times, accompanied by concentration, attaches to the form an effect by which the impediment is removed.
Second. For the warding off of nightmares, dread, evil thoughts and the impressions of jinn, the phrase "Ḥasbiya Allāhu lā ilāha illā Huwa, ʿalay-Hi tawakkaltu, wa-Huwa Rabbu al-ʿArshi al-ʿaẓīm" should be Editorial note: This chapter, with its enumeration of specific khawāṣṣ for specific phrases of the litany, is the most practical of the introductory discussions and the most likely to be misused. The author's own caution, repeated at the close of the chapter, is that the properties enumerated are properties that have been observed; they are not mechanical guarantees that the reciter may demand. The line between the legitimate use of a transmitted property and the magical instrumentalisation of a sacred text is fine but real.
The marker, in my reading, is the orientation of the reciter's heart: if it is upon God, the recitation is a supplication; if it is upon the result, the recitation has slipped into something else. The author writes for those for whom the marker is clear; the rest of us must work to make it so.
13

recited seven times before sleep, with the resolve that the seven recitations correspond to the seven heavens. The protection thus secured has been tested by the masters and is approved.
Third. For one who finds himself surrounded by enemies and in need of urgent protection, the phrase "Bismillāhi al-ladhī lā yaḍurru maʿa ismihi shayʾun fī al-arḍi wa-lā fī al-samāʾi wa-Huwa al-Samīʿu al-ʿAlīm"
should be recited three times, on rising from sleep, three times after sunset, and three times before sleep. Whoever recites this with confidence will be preserved from sudden calamity until the next recitation.
Fourth. For one whose provision (rizq) is contracted, the verses "Wa-sakhkhir lanā kulla baḥr" ("And subjugate for us every sea") should be repeated forty times daily, accompanied by giving in charity according to one's means. By the testimony of those who have practised this, the contraction is loosened and the doors of provision are opened.
Fifth. For one who is in distress at sea, or who is travelling and fears the loss of life or property, the phrase concerning the calming of the wind for Sulaymān ("Wa-sakhkhartal-rīḥa wa-l-shayāṭīna wa-l-jinna liSulaymān") should be repeated, with concentration upon the wind itself, until calm appears. This was the very practice of the Shaykh on his own voyage.
Sixth. For one who is in difficulty with rulers and those in authority, the phrase "Wa-iṭmas ʿalā wujūhi aʿdāʾinā wa-msakh-hum ʿalā makānatihim fa-lā yastaṭīʿūna al-muḍiyya wa-lā al-majīʾa ilaynā" should be recited with the form of the oppressor before the heart, until the contraction lifts. The masters caution, however, that this is to be used only when the oppressor is in fact wronging the reciter, and is not to be used to harm the innocent, for the litany has within it a sword which cuts whoever is liable to be cut.
Seventh. For the seeker of unveiling and the seeker of nearness to God, the entire litany recited daily, with full attention upon the chain (the

Source, the Prophet, the Shaykh, the reciter), is itself a road of opening, and there is no greater khāṣiyyah than this.
Eighth. For the person of distress in any matter, the litany recited twelve times in twelve days, beginning at the dawn-prayer and ending after sunset, with daily fast and seclusion, will, by the leave of God, bring the affair to its appointed answer in one of three forms: either the affair is completed as the reciter wished; or it is completed in a manner the reciter had not foreseen but which is better; or the heart of the reciter is so altered that he no longer requires the affair he had originally requested.
Ninth. Above all, the reciter must not approach the litany as a means of compelling God; he must approach it as a means of being conformed to God's will. The properties enumerated above are properties that have been observed; they are not guarantees that the reciter may demand. The Source remains free, and the litany is His servant; whoever uses the litany while remembering this is, by that very remembering, brought near.

Twelfth Discussion: On the Chains of Transmission (asānīd) of Ḥizb al-Baḥr Although the matter of the transmission has been touched upon in passing, it is fitting that a clearer statement be given here. For people of this affair the chain of transmission is not a mere technicality of scholarship; it is a living conduit of the Light. To recite the litany without being attached to the chain is to drink from a cup that has been disconnected from the source; to recite it with the chain is to drink from the spring itself.14 First. This faqīr has received this litany by way of authorisation (ijāzah) for its recitation and its transmission. He received it from his father, the Shaykh Abū Ṭāhir Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Madanī, who himself read it from a number of teachers and was given authorisation by them. Among those teachers were the Shaykh Aḥmad al-Najlī al-Aḥmadī al-Maqarrī, the Shaykh ʿAlī al-Maghribī, the Shaykh Abū al-Ṣalāḥ Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wāḥid al-Anṣārī, the Shaykh Abū Ilyās Aḥmad al-Maqarrī, and others.
Second. These teachers received the litany from their predecessors in unbroken chains, going back through the line of the Shādhilī and Mursī Shaykhs to His Excellency Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his sacred soul) himself. The chain through Imām al-Shādhilī Editorial note: The author's image of the cup and the spring repays attention. The cup is the litany itself, the form of words; the spring is the inheritance of intent and presence that flows from the original receiver, Imām al-Shādhilī, to every reciter who is connected to him by sanad. The argument, made obliquely in the chapter, is that the form of words alone is not the litany; the form of words plus the connection is the litany. From this argument follows the practical advice: that the reciter should, where possible, take ijāzah from a living shaykh in the chain; and where this is not possible, should at least recite with the conscious intention of being attached to the chain by general permission. I add:
the practice of visualising the figure of the Shaykh during recitation, which Shāh Walī Allāh recommends, is itself a way of effecting this attachment in the absence of formal ijāzah, and is one of the genuine gifts of the Naqshbandī line to the wider community of recitation.
14

passes through Shaykh Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mursī (his great khalīfah) and through other of his immediate disciples; and from al-Shādhilī it goes back to the spiritual Pole of his time, and from him to the line of the Prophet (peace be upon him).
Third. There exist many such chains in the world; their multiplicity does not weaken the litany, on the contrary, it strengthens it, for many waters from many springs are nevertheless one water by their union with the great river. The reciter is to attach himself to whichever chain has been opened to him by his own teacher; if no chain has been opened, he is at least to recite with the intention of being attached to the chain by means of the Shaykh's general permission for the people of God.
Fourth. It is the practice of this faqīr that, at the moment of recitation, he visualises the Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī seated before him; he then recites the litany while looking, with the heart, upon the Shaykh's face, until the litany takes the colour of the Shaykh's gaze. From the Shaykh he passes upward by visualisation to the Prophet (peace be upon him); from the Prophet to the Throne; from the Throne to the secret of the Most Sacred Outpouring; and from there he descends again, with his need, by the same chain. Whoever does this will find that the recitation has a wholly different taste from the recitation of one who does not.
Fifth. The litany has further chains through the NaqshbandīMujaddidī line, by way of those who have received it as a recognised wird in that order, most notably through Mawlānā Shāh Ghulām ʿAlī (raḥima-hu Allāh) and his successor Mawlānā Shāh Aḥmad Saʿīd Ṣāḥib qiblah, and (in the Rāmpūr branch) through Shāh Walī Allāh Naqshbandī Mujaddidī Rāmpūrī. The reciter who has any attachment to one of these lines should bring the relevant Shaykh to mind alongside Imām alShādhilī at the moment of recitation.
Sixth. Finally, it should be stated that there is no incompatibility between the Shādhilī provenance of the litany and its adoption by the Naqshbandī-Mujaddidī Shaykhs. The Lights are one; the litany is one;
the chains are many. He who serves at the table of the great is not concerned with the names of the cooks who set the table, he is concerned only with whether the food has come from the King.

THE PURPOSE (Maqṣad) In the Purpose, the words of Ḥizb al-Baḥr will be commented upon, beneath the literal translation, with respect to the meaning that is technically intended (the muwāfiq fiqhī), the subtle indication (ishārah laṭīfah) which descends within the breast of the gnostic, and the practical effect which is bound up with the recitation. Each major phrase or group of phrases (fiqrah) is gathered into one jamʿah; within each jamʿah the discussion is arranged into numbered sub-points so that the reciter may know in what station he stands at the moment of uttering each phrase, and toward what aspect of the Divine name he is at that moment turning.
The numbering follows the original.15
 First Jamʿah, On the Opening: "Yā ʿAlī, Yā ʿAẓīm, Yā Ḥalīm, Yā ʿAlīm" (O Most High, O Magnificent, O Forbearing, O All-Knowing) In the very beginning of the speech, by mentioning some of the special Names of God, the Shaykh has indicated the immensity of the matter and the lofty aspiration with which one should recite. These four Names are deeply connected with the disposition of the human soul (nafs nāṭiqah) and with its journey along the path.
First. The connection of the first pair (ʿAlī, ʿAẓīm) with the soul is that they free the soul from clinging to lower causes by lifting its gaze.
Editorial note: The reader will notice that Shāh Walī Allāh's commentary in the Maqṣad does three things at once for every phrase of the litany: it explains the literal meaning (translation), it indicates an inner allusion (ishārah), and it specifies a practical orientation of the heart at the moment of recitation. This three-fold structure is the crystallisation of the entire Sufi commentarial tradition: ẓāhir, bāṭin, and ʿamal, the outward, the inward, and the action. A commentary that gave only the literal meaning would be a translation;
one that gave only the inner allusion would be a meditation; one that gave only the practical orientation would be a manual. By giving all three at every step, the author transforms the litany from a text to be read into a spiritual exercise to be performed.
15

ʿAlī (the Most High) lifts the soul above its preoccupations; ʿAẓīm (the Magnificent) instils awe in place of triviality.
Second. The connection of the second pair (Ḥalīm, ʿAlīm) with the soul is that they restore the soul's confidence by reminding it of the Divine knowledge of, and patience with, its weakness. Ḥalīm (the Forbearing) instils patience and refrains the soul from haste; ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing) reminds the soul of the Divine knowledge from which nothing is hidden.
Third. The placing of the names of transcendence first and the names of nearness second is itself a dispensation of mercy: the reciter is informed that nothing in the litany may be reached by way of presumption upon the Divine intimacy alone, but that the gateway is through awe; and yet, having passed the gate, he is assured that he stands before One who is forbearing and knowing of his weakness.
Fourth. There is, in the practice of the masters, a special whispered note attached to this opening: that the reciter should pause at each Name long enough for its meaning to settle into the heart before passing to the next; should breathe out with the Name and breathe in with attention;
should not hurry. Mere repetition in haste does not yield the descent;
whereas the unhurried opening, recited with attention upon the meaning, opens the rest of the litany like a key in a well-oiled lock.
Fifth. By calling upon these four Names together, the reciter sets the soul in the condition of one who is already heard. The litany has, by these very first four words, taken him from the ordinary state into the state of supplication.

Second Jamʿah, On "Anta Rabbī wa-ʿilmuka ḥasbī" (Thou art my Lord, and Thy knowledge is sufficient for me) Here the reciter, having passed through the gate of awe and intimacy, makes formal acknowledgement of the relation that obtains between him and his Lord, and of the bare knowledge of the Lord as sufficient for the meeting of every need.
First. He says "Thou art my Lord" before he says anything about himself; for the Lord's lordship is the foundation, and the slave's slavehood is the consequence. To begin with the Lord, before mentioning any need, is the practice of the masters; whoever begins with his need has begun outside the gate.
Second. He does not say "Thy power is sufficient for me" or "Thy mercy is sufficient for me", though both would be true, but "Thy knowledge is sufficient for me": for he affirms that, the Lord knowing his case completely, no further intermediary is required. To know is to dispose; for the Lord, to know is the same as to act.
Third. This phrase is, in the practice of the gnostic, a place of special pause; the heart should fasten itself here, for if it is fastened here, the rest of the litany flows freely. Many of the early Shaykhs would repeat this phrase three or seven times before moving on, until the meaning had settled fully into the chest.
Fourth. The phrase has, additionally, a hidden effect upon the reciter himself: the more often he says "Thy knowledge is sufficient for me", the less he relies upon his own knowledge, and the freer his own heart becomes from the burden of needing to know.

Third Jamʿah, On "Niʿma al-Rabb Rabbī, wa-niʿma al-ḥasb ḥasbī" (Excellent is the Lord, my Lord; excellent is the Sufficiency, my Sufficiency) After acknowledgement comes praise: the reciter does not merely state the relation but praises it. The phrase has within it a double pleasure, the pleasure of having a Lord, and the pleasure of having that Lord as one's own.
First. "Excellent is the Lord, my Lord", the soul rejoices in its Lord.
The first phrase is a general praise; the addition of "my Lord"
particularises that general praise to the reciter himself, and converts a doctrine into an experience.
Second. "Excellent is the Sufficiency, my Sufficiency", the soul rejoices in the very fact of its needing nothing else. This double praise dissolves the residue of complaint that often clings to the heart of one who supplicates from need; for he who praises while asking has already half-received.
Third. The combination of "the Lord" and "the Sufficiency" indicates that the relation of lordship is not bare authority but is filled with provision. The Lord is also the Sufficient One; whoever has Him does not need another.
Fourth. When this phrase is recited with full presence, the gnostic experiences a certain easing in his chest, like the easing of a man who, having arrived at his own home after long travel, sets down his burden.
The phrase is therefore a place of rest within the litany.

Fourth Jamʿah, On "Tanṣuru man tashāʾu wa-Anta al-ʿAzīz al-Raḥīm" (Thou helpest whom Thou willest, and Thou art the Mighty, the Compassionate) Here, having dissolved his complaint into praise, the reciter returns to the matter of help, but the phrasing is precise.
First. He says "Thou helpest whom Thou willest", not "whom we wish", for the help is by the Lord's will, not by our claim upon Him. The slave does not approach the Lord with rights; he approaches Him with hopes. The phrase is a recognition of this fact.
Second. The combination ʿAzīz (the Mighty) and Raḥīm (the Compassionate) is, in the language of the gnostics, the marriage of jalāl (majesty) and jamāl (beauty). By the Mighty, the enemy is repelled; by the Compassionate, the believer is gathered. To recite this phrase with awareness of both faces is to invoke a complete protection.
Third. The reciter who is afraid of his enemy attaches himself to ʿAzīz; the reciter who is broken by his own weakness attaches himself to Raḥīm. The litany permits both attachments at once, for the Lord is both at once.
Fourth. It is at this phrase that the reciter releases his hold upon his preferred outcome and consigns the matter to the Divine will. He has acknowledged, praised, and now resigns. The rest of the litany proceeds upon this resignation.

Fifth Jamʿah, On "Nasʾaluka al-ʿiṣmata fī al-ḥarakāti wa-lsakanāti wa-l-kalimāti wa-l-irādāti wa-l-khaṭarāti…" (We ask of Thee preservation in our motions, our stillnesses, our words, our intentions, and our thoughts…) Here the reciter shifts from the language of relation to the language of petition. The petition is, however, not for any worldly matter first; it is for the preservation of the inward state. The masters have always insisted that this is the order of priority: first, the inner; second, the outer.
First. Five things are mentioned in turn: motions (ḥarakāt), stillnesses (sakanāt), words (kalimāt), intentions (irādāt), and thoughts (khaṭarāt).
The reciter is asking for ʿiṣmah, preservation, protection from sin and slip, in each of these. The order is from the most outward (motion) to the most inward (passing thought).
Second. What follows is then said: "min al-shukūki wa-l-ẓunūni wal-awhāmi al-sātiratī li-l-qulūbi ʿan muṭālaʿati al-ghuyūb", "from doubts, suspicions, and imaginings which veil the hearts from witnessing the Unseen." This indicates that the principal danger to ʿiṣmah is not gross sin (which the believer has already learnt to avoid) but the subtle sins of doubt, suspicion, and false imagining, which veil the heart, even while the body remains apparently in worship.
Third. It is no accident that the petition for preservation precedes the petition for help against enemies. For the gnostic knows that the worst enemy is the doubt within his own breast; the outward enemy can be repelled by the litany, but the inward enemy can only be repelled by ʿiṣmah, which is a special grace.
Fourth. The verse-fragment then mentions a particular Quranic context: "Faqad ubtuliyya al-muʾminūna wa-zulzilū zilzālan shadīdan", "and the believers were tried and shaken with a violent shaking", and "wa-idh yaqūlu al-munāfiqūna wa-lladhīna fī qulūbihim maraḍun mā waʿadanā Allāhu wa-Rasūluhu illā ghurūran", "and when the hypocrites

and those in whose hearts is a disease said, 'God and His Messenger have promised us nothing but delusion.'" The Shaykh has placed these verses here to remind the reciter that the test of doubt is the very test of the hypocrites of Madīnah; whoever recites the litany and is freed from that doubt is freed from the disease of the hypocrites.
Fifth. The reciter who pauses upon this section and prays sincerely for ʿiṣmah will find, by the leave of God, that doubts which had previously settled in his breast begin to lift; the practical effect of this fifth jamʿah is the cleansing of the heart.

Sixth Jamʿah, On "Fa-thabbitnā wa-nṣurnā wa-sakhkhir lanā hādhā al-baḥr" (So make us firm, and help us, and subjugate for us this sea) Having sought ʿiṣmah, the reciter now turns to the matter of help.
The order is: firmness first (thabbitnā), help second (unṣurnā), subjugation of the sea third (sakhkhir lanā hādhā al-baḥr).
First. Firmness (tathbīt) is the precondition of help: an unsteady servant cannot receive help, for help that descends upon a moving target is dissipated. The reciter therefore prays first to be planted, then to be aided.
Second. "Subjugate for us this sea", by which is meant, at the outward level, the sea of water; at the inward level, the sea of the world; at the further inward level, the sea of the reciter's own self. The litany subjugates all three together, for whoever can bring his own self into submission has, by that very act, brought the world and the water into submission.
Third. The reciter at this phrase visualises a great body of water, turbulent, threatening, and watches it become still as he says the word "sakhkhir". This is not magic; it is a recognition that the will of the Lord is the cause of both the turbulence and the stillness, and the litany puts the reciter into alignment with that will.
Fourth. The phrase "hādhā al-baḥr", "this sea", is to be applied by the reciter to whatever sea is presently before him. If he is on the ocean, it is the ocean; if he is in a difficulty, it is that difficulty; if he is at war with himself, it is that war. The Shaykh has used the demonstrative on purpose, that each reciter may apply it to his own state.

Seventh Jamʿah, On the Four Subjugations (sakhkharta albaḥra li-Mūsā… al-nāra li-Ibrāhīm… al-jibāla wa-l-ḥadīda liDāwūd… al-rīḥa wa-l-shayāṭīna wa-l-jinna li-Sulaymān) The Shaykh now lists four prophetic subjugations as precedents for his own petition: the parting of the sea for Mūsā, the cooling of the fire for Ibrāhīm, the softening of the iron and the praising of the mountains for Dāwūd, and the binding of the wind, the demons, and the jinn for Sulaymān. The reasoning is that of qiyās: as the four were granted, so let this fifth be granted to us.16 First. The four subjugations correspond to the four elements. The sea, water; the fire, fire; the mountain and the iron, earth; the wind, the demons, and the jinn, air (and what inhabits it). The Shaykh has thus exhausted the elemental world in his petition: "O Lord, as Thou didst subjugate every element for Thy prophets, subjugate them for us in our need."
Second. By the parting of the sea for Mūsā, the reciter prays: "Open for us a way through what appears to be a sealed obstacle." By the cooling of the fire for Ibrāhīm, the reciter prays: "Make harmless for us what was set as a harm." By the softening of the iron for Dāwūd, the reciter prays:
"Bend for us what is rigid in our affair." By the binding of the wind for Sulaymān, the reciter prays: "Take from our enemies their breath of motion and bind them in their place."
 Editorial note: The pattern of this jamʿah deserves close attention. The author maps the four prophetic miracles onto the four elements (water, fire, earth, air) and then onto the four cardinal difficulties of the human soul (the impassable barrier, the test of fire, the unyielding world, the unseen harassment). The result is that a single recitation of the four phrases of the litany engages, simultaneously, the four corners of the cosmos and the four corners of the human predicament. This is the deepest answer to the question of why the litany works: it does not address one need at one frequency, like an ordinary supplication, but engages the full structure of the cosmos and the full structure of the soul at once. To recite it with this map in mind is to recite it correctly.
16

Third. These four prophetic moments are also four states of the human soul: the soul that meets a barrier (the sea); the soul that is thrown into a fire (the test); the soul that finds the world unyielding (the iron);
and the soul that is harassed by hidden enemies (the jinn). The reciter who recognises these states in himself recites these phrases not merely as historical reminiscence but as the four medicines that the Shaykh has compounded for him.
Fourth. The Shaykh has thus, in the very middle of his litany, deposited four secret keys to the four cardinal difficulties of the human soul. Whoever knows the secret of these four keys may use them, by the leave of God, in any moment of difficulty corresponding to one of the four. The litany is, in this respect, a portable medicine-box.
Fifth. It must be stated, however, that the reciter is not, by reciting these prophetic precedents, claiming the rank of the prophets. He is rather invoking their memory before his Lord, in the manner of one servant invoking the favour of the Master toward another servant by saying:
"Thou wast generous to so-and-so; be generous to me as well."

Eighth Jamʿah, On the Universal Subjugation: "Wa-sakhkhir lanā kulla baḥrin huwa laka fī al-arḍi wa-l-samāʾ wa-l-mulki wa-l-malakūt, wa-baḥra al-dunyā wa-baḥra al-ākhirah" (And subjugate for us every sea that is Thine, in earth and heaven, in dominion and sovereignty, the sea of this world and the sea of the next) Having mentioned four particular seas (the four prophetic subjugations), the Shaykh now widens the petition to every sea: not only the seas of water, but the seas of dominion, the seas of unseen sovereignty, the sea of this world, and the sea of the next.
First. By "every sea that is Thine" the Shaykh has gathered, in a single phrase, all the seas of being: the seas of the four elements, the seas of the planetary intelligences, the seas of the angelic ranks, the seas of the divine names, and the sea of the Self. He prays that all be brought into submission to the Lord, that there be no point of being which is not, at this moment, in the hand of the Lord on behalf of the reciter.
Second. The mention of mulk (the dominion of the visible) and malakūt (the dominion of the unseen) together makes the phrase a comprehensive one: it leaves nothing out. Whoever recites it with attention has, in a sense, paid a single short visit to every realm of being and has placed it in the hand of the Lord.
Third. The further addition of "the sea of this world and the sea of the next" is the seal of completeness: the petition reaches across the boundary of death. The reciter's needs in this world are submitted; his needs in the next are also submitted. He is not asking only for safe passage on the sea today; he is asking for safe passage across the sea of the grave and the sea of the resurrection.
Fourth. The phrase concludes with: "Wa-sakhkhir lanā kulla shayʾin yā man bi-yadihi malakūtu kulli shayʾ", "And subjugate for us every thing, O Thou in whose hand is the sovereignty of every thing." This is a
recognition: I am asking from the One who already holds it. There is no presumption; there is only request.

Ninth Jamʿah, On "Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād" (the disconnected letters of Sūrat Maryam) The Shaykh inserts here the disconnected letters of Sūrat Maryam, Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād, which are recited three times. The placing of these letters at this exact point in the litany is not arbitrary; it is the deliberate use of a particular instrument.
First. These five letters are reported, in the unveilings of certain masters, to correspond to five Divine Names: K (al-Kāfī, the Sufficient), H (al-Hādī, the Guide), Y (al-Yad, the divine "hand" or care), ʿAyn (alʿAlīm or al-ʿAdl), Ṣ (al-Ṣādiq or al-Ṣamad). To recite the letters is, by the leave of God, to invoke these five names in a coded form.
Second. By placing them at this point in the litany, between the petition for universal subjugation and the petition for victory, the Shaykh has, as it were, fastened the previous petitions with a seal of five names, before opening the next petition.
Third. The recitation thrice is itself a noted practice: that any verse or formula whose effect is sought in earnest may be repeated three times to firm up its descent.
