The number three corresponds to the three states of the human being (heart, tongue, limb); to recite a phrase three times is to send it through all three at once.
Fourth. The reciter, at this moment, should turn his heart most particularly toward the Throne, for the disconnected letters are, of all parts of the litany, the most directly attached to the upper world. The other phrases descend; the disconnected letters ascend.

Tenth Jamʿah, On the Five-fold Petition: "Unṣurnā… wa-ftaḥ lanā… wa-ghfir lanā… wa-rḥamnā… wa-rzuqnā…" (Help us… open for us… forgive us… have mercy upon us… provide for us… ) After the seal of the five letters, the Shaykh now opens a five-fold petition, each line of which has the form "…fa-innaka khayru al-…"
("…for Thou art the best of those who…"). The five petitions are: help, opening, forgiveness, mercy, and provision.
First. Help (naṣr) is asked first because, in the order of the litany, the reciter has just placed himself in submission; the first need of the submitted is to be helped. Help is in turn the precondition of opening.
Second. Opening (fatḥ) is asked second because, even after help arrives, the reciter often finds doors still closed before him; he therefore asks for the opening of the doors as a separate matter. The Lord may help without opening (by giving patience), and may open without obvious help (by sudden grace); the reciter asks for both.
Third. Forgiveness (maghfirah) is asked third, at the centre of the five, because forgiveness is the hinge upon which the others turn: an unforgiven sin is a wall against help, against opening, against mercy, and against provision; the request for forgiveness, placed in the middle, removes the wall.
Fourth. Mercy (raḥmah) is asked fourth, after forgiveness, because mercy descends upon the forgiven, and provision (rizq) is asked fifth, because provision is, in the doctrine of the masters, the outermost garment of mercy. To go from forgiveness to mercy to provision is to descend the staircase of grace from its highest step to its visible base.
Fifth. Each line is sealed with "fa-innaka khayru al-…", "for Thou art the best of those who…". This is not flattery; it is recognition. The Lord is best because there is no other; and the reciter affirms this at the
end of each petition lest he, in his own mind, should imagine that some secondary cause is the actual giver.

Eleventh Jamʿah, On "Wa-hdinā wa-najjinā mina al-qawmi al-ẓālimīna" (And guide us, and deliver us from the wrongdoing folk) After the five-fold petition, the Shaykh joins together two further requests: guidance and deliverance from the wrongdoers.
First. Guidance (hidāyah) and deliverance (najāh) are paired because they are the inward and the outward of a single grace. Whoever is inwardly guided is in the way of being outwardly delivered; whoever is outwardly delivered without inward guidance has only postponed his harm.
Second. The wrongdoers (al-qawm al-ẓālimīn) are not only the political oppressor; they include the wrongdoers in one's own household, in one's own friendship, and, most subtly, the wrongdoer within one's own breast (the soul that wrongs itself). The reciter prays for deliverance from all three.
Third. The phrase combines guidance with deliverance because they support one another: a guided slave is delivered, and a delivered slave is enabled to be further guided. The two together form a self-perpetuating circle of grace.

Twelfth Jamʿah, On the Petition for the Fair Wind: "Wa-hab lanā rīḥan ṭayyibatan kamā hiya fī ʿilmika, wa-nshurhā ʿalaynā min khazāʾini raḥmatika, wa-ḥmilnā bihā ḥamla alkarāmati maʿa al-salāmati wa-l-ʿāfiyati fī al-dīni wa-l-dunyā wa-l-ākhirah"
Now begins the most concretely "sea-going" portion of the litany:
the petition for a fair wind. The phrase has within it three movements:
grant the wind, unfurl it upon us, carry us by it.
First. "Grant us a fair wind, as it is in Thy knowledge", the reciter does not specify what wind he wants; he submits to the Lord's knowledge of what wind would in fact be fair for him. He has thus placed his judgement under the Lord's, in the very moment of asking. This is one of the secrets of acceptance: the petition that is most likely to be granted is the one that does not over-specify.
Second. "Unfurl it upon us from the treasuries of Thy mercy", by mentioning the treasuries (khazāʾin), the reciter acknowledges that the source of the wind is not in the world but in a hidden storehouse. The wind is not weather; it is mercy taking the form of weather.
Third. "Carry us by it with the carrying of honour", not merely safe carrying, but honourable carrying. The reciter has, in this phrase, asked for more than mere safety; he has asked for safety with dignity, with comfort, with peace of heart.
Fourth. "With safety and well-being in religion, in this world, and in the next", the petition is then sealed across all three domains. The reciter has not asked merely for a safe trip; he has asked for the journey to leave his religion intact, his worldly affairs in order, and his next-world standing improved.

Fifth. "Verily Thou art powerful over all things", and this is the seal upon the petition: the reminder that what has been asked is, for the One asked, a small thing. Whoever asks while remembering this is heard.

Thirteenth Jamʿah, On the Petition for the Affairs of the Journey: "Allāhumma yassir lanā umūranā maʿa al-rāḥati liqulūbinā wa-abdāninā wa-l-salāmati wa-l-ʿāfiyati fī dīninā wa-dunyānā, wa-kun lanā ṣāḥiban fī safarinā wa-khalīfatan fī ahlinā"
After the wind, the Shaykh asks for the journey itself to be eased; and not only the outward journey but the inward states that accompany it.
First. "Ease for us our affairs", the request is for taysīr, easing. The reciter does not ask that the affair be removed; he asks that it be made easy. The believer is to expect affairs in this life; he is to expect that they be made easy by his Lord.
Second. "Together with rest for our hearts and our bodies", the petition specifies that the easing be inward as well as outward. Many are eased outwardly while their hearts remain in turmoil; the reciter prays not to be one of these.
Third. "And safety and well-being in our religion and in our world", again, the dual domain. The journey may be safe in the outward and dangerous in the religious; the reciter prays for both kinds of safety together.
Fourth. "And be Thou our companion in our journey, and a successor in our families", this is the famous prophetic supplication for travel. The Shaykh has joined it to the litany at the appropriate place. The Lord is asked to be "with us" while we are on the road, and "in our place" while we are absent from those we have left behind.

Fourteenth Jamʿah, On the Effacement of the Faces of the Enemies: "Wa-ṭmis ʿalā wujūhi aʿdāʾinā wa-msakh-hum ʿalā makānatihim fa-lā yastaṭīʿūna al-muḍiyya wa-lā al-majīʾa ilaynā"
Having placed his journey in the Lord's care, the reciter now turns to the enemies who would obstruct him. The petition is for two things: that their faces be effaced, and that they be paralysed in their place.
First. "Efface the faces of our enemies", by "face" is meant the outward power of the enemy, the apparatus by which he confronts the believer. The petition is that this apparatus be deprived of its working:
the eye that watches, the tongue that schemes, the ear that listens for advantage.
Second. "And paralyse them in their place", that they be unable to move forward (against the believer) or backward (away from the consequences of their previous wrong). They are to be held in their station, like a man in a dream who cannot move.
Third. It must be added (and the masters insist on this) that the petition is for protection of the believer from the enemy, not for the harm of any innocent person. The reciter who recites this phrase against an innocent person, falsely calling that person an enemy, has aimed the litany at himself.
Fourth. Then come the two Quranic verses: "And had We willed, We would have effaced their eyes…" and "And had We willed, We would have transformed them in their place…". These are not new petitions; they are confirmations of what has just been asked, drawn from the speech of God Himself. The Shaykh has joined the petition with the divine confirmation.

Fifteenth Jamʿah, On the Verses of Yā Sīn: "Yā Sīn, wa-lQurʾāni al-ḥakīm…" through "…wa-jaʿalnā min bayni aydīhim saddan wa-min khalfihim saddan fa-aghshaynāhum fa-hum lā yubṣirūn"
The Shaykh now gathers, in this section of the litany, the famous verses from the opening of Sūrat Yā Sīn. These are the verses that the people of God have, in every age, used as a wall around themselves and their dependents.
First. "Yā Sīn, by the Wise Quran, verily thou art among the messengers, upon a straight path", these opening verses establish the reality of the prophetic mission. The reciter who recites them, even if he is not himself a prophet, places himself within the protection of the prophetic mission, as a member of the community for which it was sent.
Second. "The revelation of the Mighty, the Compassionate", the same combination of jalāl and jamāl which opened the litany now reappears in the middle. The Shaykh has placed it twice on purpose: once at the beginning (as the gate), and once at the middle (as the wall).
Third. "Truly We have placed upon their necks shackles up to their chins, so they are kept upright; and We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and We have covered them, so they cannot see", these verses are recited with the visualisation of the actual placing of these barriers around the enemy. The Shaykh's followers used to recite this with the form of the enemy before them, watching the barriers descend.
Fourth. It is reported that whoever, before going to bed, recites these verses three times, with the visualisation of the barriers being placed around his house, barriers before, barriers behind, a covering above, will sleep through the night without disturbance from any unseen force, and his sleep will be a sleep of mercy. Many of the Shādhilī Shaykhs have practised this, and it is approved.

Sixteenth Jamʿah, On the Humbling of the Faces: "Shāhati alwujūh" (recited three times) and "Wa-ʿanati al-wujūhu li-lḤayyi al-Qayyūm, wa-qad khāba man ḥamala ẓulman"
"The faces are abased", recited three times, this is one of the most concentrated phrases in the litany. The Shaykh has used the prophetic words from Badr, when the Prophet (peace be upon him) cast a handful of pebbles toward the unbelievers, saying "shāhati al-wujūh" ("the faces are abased"), and a wind threw the pebbles in their eyes.
First. The repetition three times follows the prophetic precedent. The Shaykh has not added or subtracted; he has placed the prophetic phrase, in its prophetic form, into his own litany. The reciter who recites these three repetitions partakes, by way of attachment, in the very battle of Badr.
Second. "And the faces are humbled before the Living, the SelfSubsisting", this is a Quranic phrase concerning the Day of Resurrection.
By placing it after the prophetic "shāhati al-wujūh", the Shaykh has joined the abasement of the enemy in this world to the abasement of every wrongdoer in the next. The two abasements are linked.
Third. "And he who carries injustice has indeed failed", this is the verdict upon the wrongdoer. By saying it, the reciter does not himself condemn anyone; he reads aloud the verdict that the Lord has already pronounced. The reciter is, in a sense, the herald of a sentence already given.

Seventeenth Jamʿah, On the Disconnected Letters "Ṭā Sīn… Ḥā Mīm… ʿAyn Sīn Qāf" and the verse of the Two Seas The Shaykh now inserts the disconnected letters from several different sūrahs, Ṭā Sīn (from al-Naml), Ḥā Mīm and ʿAyn Sīn Qāf (from al-Shūrā), followed by the verse "He has loosed the two seas which meet, between them is a barrier they do not transgress."
First. These disconnected letters are again coded names of the Lord, in the manner mentioned in the ninth mabhath of the introduction. By placing them here, after the abasement of the enemy and before the verse of the two seas, the Shaykh has, as it were, gathered the names that govern this section under one banner.
Second. The verse of the two seas, "Maraja al-baḥrayn yaltaqiyān, baynahumā barzakhun lā yabghiyān", is recited at this point as a barrier between the believer and his enemy. As the two seas meet but do not mix because of the barzakh between them, so let the believer and the enemy meet but be kept apart by an unseen barrier.
Third. This is one of the most subtle uses of Quranic verses in the litany: the verse, which in its outward sense describes a phenomenon of the natural world, is here applied to the relation between two persons.
The Shaykh has read in the verse a metaphor that the Lord Himself has provided. Whoever recites the verse with this application participates in the metaphor.

Eighteenth Jamʿah, On the Sevenfold "Ḥā Mīm" and the Sealing Verse: "Ḥumma al-amru, wa-jāʾa al-naṣru, fa-ʿalaynā lā yunṣarūn"
Now the Shaykh recites "Ḥā Mīm" seven times, and seals the recitation with: "The matter has been decreed; help has come; against us they shall not be victorious."
First. Why "Ḥā Mīm" seven times? Because the Quran has seven sūrahs whose openings begin with these letters (the Ḥawāmīm: alMuʾmin, Fuṣṣilat, al-Shūrā, al-Zukhruf, al-Dukhān, al-Jāthiyah, alAḥqāf). To recite the letters seven times is to invoke the protection of the seven sūrahs at one stroke.
Second. The Companions, in the wars of the early Muslim community, are reported to have recited these letters as a wird of victory.
The Shaykh has gathered the practice of the early community and woven it into his litany at this place.
Third. "The matter has been decreed; help has come; against us they shall not be victorious", this is, in the language of the people of fal, a fixed sentence. The reciter who comes to this point in the litany has, by his recitation, been given a sentence of victory; the rest of the litany is its development.
Fourth. Each of the three clauses is a separate annunciation: (1) the affair has been completed in the unseen, i.e., the answer has already been written; (2) help has come, i.e., the answer is on its way; (3) they shall not overcome us, i.e., the enemy is already defeated, even if not yet visibly so.

Nineteenth Jamʿah, On "Ḥā Mīm, tanzīlu al-Kitābi mina Allāhi al-ʿAzīzi al-ʿAlīm, ghāfiri al-dhanbi wa-qābili altawb…"
The Shaykh now recites the opening of Sūrat Ghāfir (the second of the Ḥawāmīm), with its enumeration of seven Divine Names: al-ʿAzīz (the Mighty), al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing), Ghāfir al-dhanb (the Forgiver of sin), Qābil al-tawb (the Acceptor of repentance), Shadīd al-ʿiqāb (severe in punishment), Dhū al-ṭawl (Possessor of bounty), Lā ilāha illā Huwa, ilayhi al-maṣīr ("There is no god but He; unto Him is the return").
First. Seven Names are gathered together in this single verse, and the believer who pays close attention will see that they alternate between names of mercy and names of severity: Mighty (severity), All-Knowing (knowledge), Forgiver (mercy), Acceptor (mercy), Severe in Punishment (severity), Possessor of Bounty (mercy), and the seal: there is no god but He.
Second. By placing this verse here, the Shaykh has reminded the reciter that the same Lord who repels the enemy is the Lord who forgives the reciter himself. The mercy and the severity are not two separate Lords;
they are two aspects of one Lord, used in different respects. The reciter, having just asked for the abasement of his enemy, is reminded that he himself is in need of mercy.
Third. The seal, "There is no god but He; unto Him is the homecoming", turns the reciter inward toward his own end. He has, throughout the litany, been concerned with the affairs of the journey; this seal reminds him of the journey beyond the journey.

Twentieth Jamʿah, On the Concluding Formula: "Bismillāhi al-ladhī lā yaḍurru maʿa ismihi shayʾun fī al-arḍi wa-lā fī alsamāʾi, wa-Huwa al-Samīʿu al-ʿAlīm. Lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāhi al-ʿAliyyi al-ʿAẓīm"
The litany closes with the famous prophetic seal: "In the Name of God, with whose Name nothing in earth or heaven is harmed; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. There is no power and no strength save in God, the Most High, the Magnificent."17 First. The first part is the prophetic supplication for protection from the harm of the day and the night. It is a Hadith of the Prophet (peace be upon him) that whoever recites this three times in the morning and three times in the evening will be protected from sudden harm. The Shaykh has placed it at the seal of his litany so that the litany ends, as it began, in the prophetic precedent.
Second. The second part, "There is no power and no strength save in God, the Most High, the Magnificent", is the great formula of resignation (taslīm). The litany ends not with the believer's claim but with his renunciation of all claim. He has asked; he has placed; he has been heard;
and now he says, "None of this is my power. There is no power and no strength save in God."
Third. Notice that the seal returns to the same two Names with which the litany opened: "al-ʿAlī al-ʿAẓīm", the Most High and the Magnificent.
The litany has thus traced a circle: it began at the Most High and the Editorial note: The author's observation, drawn out in the third sub-point below, that the litany begins and ends with the same two Names (al-ʿAlī, al-ʿAẓīm), is one of those structural insights that, once seen, cannot be unseen. The litany is not a sequence; it is a circle. The reciter goes out from awe through intimacy back into awe; the gnostic's spiritual life is not a march from a starting point to a goal but a continual return to the same point at deeper and deeper levels. This is, I venture, the deepest single observation in the Ḥawāmiʿ, and the one that turns the work from a commentary upon the words of a litany into a commentary upon the structure of the spiritual life itself.
17

Magnificent; it ended at the Most High and the Magnificent. The reciter has gone out from these and returned to these.
Fourth. This circular structure, opening in awe, descending into intimacy, ascending again into awe, is itself a teaching: the gnostic's life is never a single linear movement but a continual return. The litany, recited daily, plants this pattern of return into the heart of the reciter, until his very breathing follows it.

THE CONCLUSION (Khātimah) The Purpose having been completed by means of these many discussions of the verses of the litany, and we having now arrived at this point, that the commentary upon Ḥizb al-Baḥr is concluded, we conclude with three brief observations on the manner of its persistent recitation.
First. Some of the earlier scholars have said: whoever wishes to recite Ḥizb al-Baḥr in its complete form should, before recitation, observe its zakāh [ruhaniyat riyadah], by leaving off the gross and subtle prohibited acts (jalālī and jamālī) for that day, and should fast that day;
should keep ablution, sit toward the qiblah, and recite the litany twice between dawn and sunrise, and once after each of the five prayers, and twice at the time of sleeping. He who does this, twelve days successively, with full faith and presence, God Most High will draw out for him the secrets of the litany, will make plain to him its inward meanings, and will guarantee for him acceptance of his three principal needs in this world and his entry beneath the protection of the litany in the next.
Second. It is a general practice of the masters of the path that, after completing the recitation, the reciter should remain in his place for some moments without speaking, for the Light of the litany is descending upon him in those moments, and any speech disperses it. He should turn his attention inward, take a few breaths in silence, and then rise. The benefit of this brief silence is great; the loss caused by neglecting it is also significant.
Third. The recitation of Ḥizb al-Baḥr is a practice of the way; it is not a magical formula divorced from sincerity and right belief. Whoever recites it in mockery, or in arrogance, or in dependence upon the recitation rather than upon God, will not find in it what the sincere find. Whoever recites it as the masters have recited it, with the heart upon God, the eye upon the meaning, the body in purity, and the tongue in clarity, will find in it, by the leave of God, the very thing the masters have found.
And our final word is: praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds, and peace and blessings of God upon our master Muḥammad and upon his family and Companions altogether.

Method of Reciting Ḥizb al-Baḥr and Discharging its Zakāh Be it known that whoever wishes to recite the Duʿāʾ Ḥizb al-Baḥr in its complete form, in observance of its five conditions, with the giving of its zakāh, for the type of withdrawal (rajʿah), that is, for protection from destruction, must observe the following.18
 The Five Conditions Condition One: that the supplicant bear no rancour (kīna) toward any of the slaves of God who are people of Islam, neither outwardly (ẓāhiran) nor inwardly (bāṭinan).
Condition Two: that he leave off the prohibited acts of the animal nature (ḥaywānāt-i jalālī wa jamālī), both gross and subtle, both of dominance and of beauty, for the duration of the practice.
Condition Three: that, having bathed in ritual purity, he wear a plain white garment in the manner of one entering iḥrām for the pilgrimage.
The simplicity of dress is itself part of the consecration of the practice.
Condition Four: that he keep a fast that day, and observe iʿtikāf (retreat) in the mosque.
 Editorial note: The very concept that a litany has a zakāh, alms or a tithe, is one of the unsung treasures of the Sufi tradition (in ruhaninyat terms a riyadah). The doctrine, briefly stated, is that any spiritual instrument of real power, the great supplications, the litanies of the masters, the recitations transmitted with sanad, has within it efficacy that requires a corresponding offering on the part of the reciter, lest the recitation be received without due acknowledgement. The zakāh is not a price for the litany; it is the discipline that proves the reciter worthy of receiving it. The reader will find that the conditions enumerated below are not arbitrary purity-rules but a remarkably integrated programme of inward and outward consecration, by which the reciter is brought, in body and in spirit, into a condition fit for the descent of the litany's blessing.
18

Condition Five: that he renew his ablution immediately if it should break, and remain in a state of ritual purity throughout the practice.
 The Material Preparations: Bread, Salt, and Water In addition to the five inward conditions, the masters have specified material preparations which constitute the outer body of the zakāh. These are not arbitrary; each carries a meaning, and together they form a single act of consecration.19 First, the bath. The reciter is instructed to perform his ghusl using river water (ab-i daryā), not standing water from a household reservoir.
The flowing water of the river represents the flowing of the litany itself;
to bathe in it is to begin the practice already attached to that flow.
Second, the loaf. For the food that he will take during the practice, only one loaf of bread (rōṭī) is to be prepared. It is to be kneaded with Lahori salt (namak-i Lāhōrī), that is, rock salt of the well-known kind, and washed with river water before baking.
Third, the firewood. The wood used to bake the loaf must be examined: care is to be taken that it contain no insects or worms (kīṛē waghairah). The reasoning of the masters is twofold: first, that no living thing be incidentally killed in the kindling of the fire of the practice;
second, that the bread be kept free of any element of impurity, however small.
Editorial note: The reader unfamiliar with the genre may find these material preparations, river water for the ghusl, a single loaf of bread baked with rock salt, firewood examined for the absence of insects, faintly bizarre. They are not. They belong to a long Indo-Persian Sufi tradition of material consecration, in which the practical components of a spiritual practice are themselves brought to a condition of purity that mirrors the inward purity required of the practitioner. The river water is alive in a way that standing water is not; the rock salt is the ancient and uncontaminated salt of the subcontinent, mined from beds laid down before any human technology touched them; the firewood free of insects ensures that the fire of consecration is not lit at the cost of any creature's life. Each preparation is a small affirmation that the practice is reverent at every stage, in its smallest material details as well as in its grandest spiritual orientations.
19

Fourth, the duration of the diet. After the loaf is baked, for three days the reciter is to eat nothing besides this single loaf, breaking his fast at the appointed times only with this bread. The simplification of the diet is itself a discipline that frees the soul for the recitation.
 The Order of the Recitation The order proper begins after the inward and outward preparations have been made. Each step has its appointed place in the sequence.
First. The reciter performs full ablution (ghusl) with river water, and dons the simple garment described above.
Second. He performs two cycles of nafl prayer (dū-gāna), in which he recites the noble Sūrat al-Fātiḥah and the noble Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ five times each, five repetitions of each, in observance of the practice transmitted in this line. The reward of these recitations is to be conveyed (through niyyah of īṣāl-i thawāb) to two recipients: first, to the soul of His Excellency the Author of the litany, Imām Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his soul); and second, to the souls of all those, Shaykhs, ancestors, and supporters, who lend assistance to the reciter on the path.
Third. After the closing salām of the prayer, the reciter takes refuge with God Most High and mentions, in his own words, the particular need for which he is undertaking the practice.
Fourth. He then recites the entire Ḥizb al-Baḥr once. If any phrase among its phrases corresponds particularly to his need, he is to pause at that phrase and repeat it three, seven, or twelve times, these being the numbers most often used by the masters, with attention turned upon the need and confidence in the answer. The seventeenfold repetition is also approved for matters of urgency, as detailed in the section on particular purposes.

Fifth. Throughout the recitation he is to keep before his heart the blessed soul (rūḥ-i mubārak) of His Excellency Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan alShādhilī (may God sanctify his soul), in the manner described in the eleventh and twelfth mabāḥith of the introduction. The visualisation is not to be exaggerated nor neglected; it is to be steady.
Sixth. After completing the recitation he should remain seated in silence for a brief while, for the Light of the litany is descending upon him in those moments, then rise.
 The Recitation after Each Prayer The litany is to be recited after each of the five obligatory prayers throughout the duration of the practice. In particular, the recitations after ʿaṣr and after maghrib are emphasised; the masters consider these two among the most powerful times for the descent of the answer. The reciter who is unable to manage all five may at least preserve these two.
 The Daily Practice and Numerical Counts Two principal daily practices are transmitted from the masters of this line:
First. The reciter performs ghusl daily and offers two rakʿahs each day, after which he recites the litany twenty-one times in a single sitting.
Second. Alternatively, during the twelve days of the waxing of the moon (urūj-i māh, that is, from the first to the twelfth of the lunar month), he recites the litany once each day, with full attention.
The first practice is suited to one with leisure for an extended daily session; the second is suited to one whose circumstances permit only a single daily recitation, and who wishes to take advantage of the special blessing transmitted with the waxing of the moon. Either is valid; both are approved. And God knows best, and His knowledge is most complete.

The Daʿwah at Completion On the completion of the practice, whether at the end of the threeday intensive, the twelve-day cycle, or the forty-day continuous practice, the reciter is to hold a daʿwah: that is, a charitable meal in which he feeds the poor, the friends of the path, and those whom he has invited. The food is to be of his own provision; the intention is to convey reward to the same souls to whom the opening recitations were conveyed.
This daʿwah is itself part of the zakāh of the litany, for the zakāh is not only the abandonment of forbidden acts and the keeping of the fast, but also the active giving of food to the deserving. Whoever omits the daʿwah at the close has discharged only half the zakāh; whoever observes it has discharged the whole.
 It is reported that the reciter who maintains this complete practice for forty days continuously will see open results; and that whoever maintains it as an ongoing periodic practice (twelve days each lunar month, for example) will find his affairs arranged for him without manifest cause, the doors of provision opened, his enemies turned away, his journey safeguarded, and his heart at rest. And God knows best, and His knowledge is most complete.

Method of Reciting Ḥizb al-Baḥr for the Attainment of Particular Purposes (maqāṣid makhṣūṣah) If any person is helpless in some matter and there is no apparent way for it to be accomplished, he should, in a clean, pure, empty place, perform two cycles (rakʿahs) of prayer; and after the closing salām of the prayer, recite Ḥizb al-Baḥr in the manner described below according to the particular purpose. By the leave of God Most High, the affair will be made easy. The masters have transmitted, for each of the principal needs, a specific protocol consisting of: (1) the number of recitations; (2) the phrase of the litany at which a special pause and repetition are to be made;
(3) a Quranic verse to be added thereafter; and (4) a particular formula of supplication to be uttered at the end.20
 In what follows, the protocols for the principal needs are given. The reciter is to receive these as transmitted guidance and to apply them with sincerity. The phrase "so-and-so son of so-and-so" (fulān ibn fulān) means that the reciter should mention the actual name of the person concerned, with the name of his father, in place of the formula.
 For the Attainment of Love and Friendship (li-jalb almaḥabbah) Editorial note: The protocols that follow have been transmitted in the NaqshbandīMujaddidī Rāmpūrī line and are contained in the Karachi printing of the Sharḥ. The reader should approach them with two cautions: first, that they are not magical formulae, the four-fold structure they share (count plus phrase plus verse plus supplication) is precisely the structure of a complete supplication, with the litany serving as the inner engine; second, that the protocols for repulsion (the tying of enemy tongues, the imprecation against oppressors) are sharp instruments and must not be turned against any innocent person. The author and the present translator both repeat this caution because it is so often ignored. The litany has within it a sword. Whoever uses it against the innocent has aimed it at himself.
20

Recite the litany twelve times, or seven times, or five times, according to the urgency of the matter. The recitation may be made over rose-water (ʿarq-i gulāb), which is afterward drunk by the reciter or, where lawful, presented to the one whose love is sought. When the reciter reaches the phrase "Wa-hab lanā rīḥan ṭayyibatan…" ("And grant us a fair wind…"), let him pause and repeat the phrase seventeen times. Then let him recite the verse: "Yuḥibbū-nahum ka-ḥubbi-llāh, wa-lladhīna āmanū ashaddu ḥubban li-llāh" ("They love them as the love due to God; but those who believe are stronger in love for God," Q 2:165). Then let him say: "O God, create love and friendship of so-and-so son of so-and-so within the heart of so-and-so son of so-and-so. Amen." Let him persist in this for twelve days, and on each of those days the recitation may be made with the visualisation of the desired form before the heart.
For the Tying of the Tongues of Enemies (li-rabṭ al-alsunah)
For twelve days, three times each day, the reciter recites the litany. When he reaches the phrase "Wa-ṭmis ʿalā wujūhi aʿdāʾinā…" ("And efface the faces of our enemies…") or the phrase "Shāhati al-wujūh" ("The faces are abased"), let him pause and repeat that phrase seventeen times. Then let him recite: "Yā Qāhir, dhī al-baṭsh al-shadīd, alladhī lā yuṭāqu intiqāmuh, yā Qāhir, khudh, khudh" ("O Subduer, possessor of severe seizure, whose vengeance cannot be withstood, O Subduer, take, take"). Let him then call upon God to bring upon so-and-so son of so-and-so a sevenfold wrath, that the eye, the tongue, and the heart of the enemy be turned away from him within twelve days. The Shaykhs add the strict caution that this is to be used only against an actual oppressor, never against an innocent person, for the litany carries within it a sword which cuts whoever is liable to be cut, and one who turns it against an innocent has aimed it at himself.

For Healing from Illness (li-shifāʾ al-amrāḍ) For healing, whether of oneself or of another, let the reciter recite the litany twelve times daily for twelve days. When he reaches the phrase "Bismillāhi al-ladhī lā yaḍurru maʿa ismihi shayʾun fī al-arḍi wa-lā fī alsamāʾi, wa-Huwa al-Samīʿu al-ʿAlīm" ("In the Name of God, with whose Name nothing in earth or heaven is harmed; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing"), let him pause and repeat the phrase seventeen times.
Then let him recite the verse:
 "Wa-nunazzilu mina al-Qurʾāni mā huwa shifāʾun wa-raḥmatun li-lmuʾminīn" ("And We send down of the Qurʾān that which is healing and mercy for the believers," Q 17:82).
Then let him say: "Yā Shāfī, grant healing to so-and-so son of soand-so, from all illness and from the duration of [his] being [afflicted]."
And every day, morning and evening, let him recite seven times each, slowly and carefully (ṭhīr ṭhīr kar, with deliberation, not in haste). After the completion of the practice, let him hold a daʿwah; and when he returns to his home, let him recite this duʿāʾ once within the home itself, that the blessing be sealed upon the house.
 For Safety on the Road and Peace of Travel (li-amn al-rāh wasalāmat al-safar) Before the traveller departs, let him observe this practice for three days. On each of those three days, with the condition of the safe arrival held in his heart, let him recite the duʿāʾ twelve times daily. When he reaches the phrase containing "Iknā kufanā humma takhalliṣ-nā" or "Yā Ḥafīẓ, iḥfaẓ-nī min jamīʿ al-baliyyāt" or "Yā Arḥam al-Rāḥimīn", these being the protective phrases of the journey, let him pause and repeat the

phrase seventeen times. The Shaykhs add: if the traveller is going by sea, this practice is especially to be observed; for the litany was originally inspired upon the sea, and its blessing returns most strongly to the sea.
 For the Protection of a Boat or Vessel in Distress (li-ḥifẓ alsafīnah) If the boat is already on the journey and meets with difficulty, a contrary wind, a threatening pirate vessel, a great wave, or any other peril, let the one in charge recite the litany seventeen times daily until safety is restored. When he reaches the phrase "Wa-sakhkhir lanā hādhā al-baḥr" ("And subjugate for us this sea"), let him pause and repeat it seventeen times, and then say:
 "Yā Ḥafīẓ, iḥfaẓ-nā min jamīʿ al-baliyyāt, yā Arḥam al-Rāḥimīn" ("O Preserver, preserve us from all calamities, O Most Merciful of the merciful").
 This is the very practice that Imām al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his soul) employed upon his own voyage when the contrary wind arose; and many of his followers have used it after him with the same effect.
 For the Resolution of Strife and Conflict (li-fitnah) Where strife has broken out, between the reciter and another, or among parties for whom the reciter prays, let him recite the litany seventeen times daily for three days. When he reaches the verse-section concerning the descent of mercy and grace, let him pause and repeat the phrase seventeen times, and then say:
 "Allāhumma ikfī-nī kulli ḥarāmika, wa-aghni-nī bi-faḍlika ʿamman siwāk" ("O God, suffice me through Your lawful so as to free me from Your forbidden, and enrich me through Your bounty so as to free me from depending upon any besides You").

For Expansion of the Chest, Increase of Intellect, and Inward Tranquility (li-inshirāḥ al-ṣadr) For the expansion of the chest, the increase of understanding, and the dwelling of tranquility in the soul, that is, for the inward graces, let the reciter recite, for three days, over sweet rose-water (or with three sweet items present, according to one transmission). When he reaches the phrase "Qad nazala fī al-Kitābi mā huwa shifāʾ" ("What has been sent down in the Book is a healing"), let him pause and repeat the phrase seventeen times, or, in the more demanding version transmitted by some, seven sets of seventeen, and then say:
 "Rabbī ishraḥ lī ṣadrī" ("My Lord, expand for me my breast," Q 20:25).
This practice should be done daily, on an empty stomach (nahārmūnh, that is, before any food has been taken), so that the heart may be opened and the understanding increased. Persistence is more important than the count; whoever continues this practice for an extended period will find, by the leave of God, that his inward darkness lifts and his outward affairs are clarified.
 For Perfect Gnosis and Overpowering Spiritual State (likamāl al-maʿrifah wa-ghalabat al-ḥāl) For the seeker of perfect knowledge of God and the descent of an overpowering spiritual state, these being the highest of the purposes for which the litany is recited, let the reciter recite the litany once each day for three days. After the third day, let him sit in seclusion (khilwah) and watch with the heart for the descent. The masters caution that no number is fixed for this purpose, for the descent of maʿrifah is at the will of the Lord, not at the will of the seeker; only sincerity, persistence, and the freeing of the heart from all but God will, by the leave of God, open the door.

And God knows best the truth of what has been said. The reciter is to take what has been transmitted, to apply it with sincerity, and to wait upon the Lord with patience. The litany has not failed those who have approached it as has been described; and whoever finds in himself a defect of result should look first to a defect in his own condition before doubting the litany.
 And God knows best, and His knowledge is most complete; and praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds.

Indications (ishārāt) attached to the Phrases of Ḥizb al-Baḥr The phrases of the litany have, attached to them in the practice of the masters, certain indications which the reciter should keep in mind at the moment of recitation, that the recitation may be accompanied by an inward orientation appropriate to the phrase. The letters of the litany run from the first letter of "Yā" to the last letter of "al-ʿAẓīm"; let the reciter visualise, at each major place, the indication that has been transmitted:
At "Yā ʿAlī, Yā ʿAẓīm": let him direct his heart upward, toward the Throne, and efface from his thought every secondary cause.
At "Anta Rabbī, wa-ʿilmuka ḥasbī": let him settle into the Lord's knowledge as into a sufficient cover.
At "Niʿma al-Rabb Rabbī": let him rest in the relation as one rests in his own home after travel.
At "Tanṣuru man tashāʾu": let him release his hold upon his preferred outcome and consign the matter to the Divine will.
At the petition for ʿiṣmah: let him survey his own movements and stillnesses, words, intentions, and passing thoughts, and place each, one by one, into the Lord's care.
At the mention of the four prophetic subjugations: let him visualise, in turn: the parting of the sea before Mūsā; the cooling of the fire around Ibrāhīm; the softening of the iron in the hands of Dāwūd; and the binding of the wind and the demons by Sulaymān.
At "Wa-sakhkhir lanā kulla baḥr": let him visualise the three seas, of his own self, of the world, and of the unseen, and submit all three to the Lord of the seas.

At the disconnected letters "Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād": let him direct his heart most particularly toward the Throne, repeating the letters three times slowly, with a pause for each.
At the five-fold petition (help, opening, forgiveness, mercy, provision): let him bring to mind, with each petition, the corresponding need in his own life.
At "Wa-hab lanā rīḥan ṭayyibah": let him visualise a fair wind upon the sea of his affair, sweeping it forward.
At "Wa-ṭmis ʿalā wujūhi aʿdāʾinā": let him visualise the face of the oppressor effaced and the oppressor paralysed in his place, taking care that the visualisation is not extended to any innocent person.
At the verses of Yā Sīn: let him visualise four walls being placed around himself and his dependents: a wall before, a wall behind, a wall to the right, a wall to the left, and a covering above.
At "Shāhati al-wujūh": let him visualise the three repetitions as three pebbles being cast at the enemies, after the prophetic precedent of Badr.
At the sevenfold "Ḥā Mīm": let him invoke the protection of the seven Ḥawāmīm sūrahs, one with each utterance.
At the seal "Wa-Huwa al-ʿAlī al-ʿAẓīm": let him return the whole affair to the One Most High, the Magnificent, and rest.
Whoever recites the litany with these indications kept in mind will find, by the leave of God, that the recitation acquires a wholly different taste from a recitation done without them. It is the difference between travelling a road in the dark and travelling the same road by daylight.

Duʿāʾ Ḥizb al-Naṣr (The Litany of Victory, also called Ḥizb al-Qahr, the Litany of Subjugation)
 Some have called Ḥizb al-Naṣr also "Ḥizb al-Qahr" (the Litany of Subjugation). Mawlānā Sayyidī Imām Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God have mercy upon him) is reported to have said concerning it: "This is among the most weighty of swords against the wrongdoers; and the most likely supplication, in respect of acceptance, has nothing closer than this."
 The mode of its recitation is as follows. After the night-prayer (ʿishāʾ), the reciter should make ablution and pray two cycles of prayer;
sit composed and present-of-heart; and recite the seven verses of "Ḥasbiya Allāhu wa-niʿma al-Wakīl" four hundred and fifty times. When he completes that count he should sit in his place and recite the litany once. He may also recite the litany alone, without the foregoing four hundred and fifty repetitions; this latter form being suitable for daily practice.
Some of the gnostics have practised this and have testified that they have witnessed by it astonishing relief from sieges and oppressors; some have been ruined by reciting it against another while the other was not deserving of ruin (for it carries a sword to whoever is liable to be cut).
Whoever recites it for his own protection alone, without imprecation upon any specific person, finds in it a benefit of repulsion.

Biographical Note on the Authors and the Transmission The original commentary, Ḥawāmiʿ, was composed in Persian by way of inspiration (ilhām) by the ʿārif bi-llāh Mawlānā Shāh Walī Allāh Muḥaddith of Delhi (may God have mercy upon him), one of the foremost ʿārifs of the Indian sub-continent in his age. He drew upon the inheritance of the Shādhilī way and the Naqshbandī-Mujaddidī line, and his commentary is among the most concentrated meditations upon the Ḥizb in any language.21 The author (or rather receiver) of the original litany, Ḥizb al-Baḥr itself, is Imām Abū al-Ḥasan al-Shādhilī (may God sanctify his soul), the founder of the Shādhilī way. He passed away in the seventh century of the Hijrah; his tomb is in the desert of Ḥumaythirah, in upper Egypt, on the road to the Red Sea, and is well-known and visited.
The author of the litany Ḥizb al-Naṣr (also called Ḥizb al-Qahr) is, according to the most reliable transmission, also Imām al-Shādhilī himself; some have attributed it instead to Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mursī, his great khalīfah. The two attributions are not contradictory: Sufi litanies often pass back and forth between the master and the disciple in just this

 It is reported in the present recension, by a chain transmitted through the Naqshbandī-Mujaddidī line, going through Mawlānā Shāh Aḥmad Saʿīd Ṣāḥib qiblah, who received from Mawlānā Shāh Ghulām ʿAlī (raḥima-hu Allāh), who received in turn from his predecessors back to the line of Imām al-Shādhilī, that Imām al-Shādhilī, while a destitute traveller in the deserts near Cairo, received an inspiration concerning the search for a ship that would take him to perform the Ḥajj. Although none was apparently available, he was inspired to wait at the port; an unexpected ship arrived, the captain of which (a Christian by religion at that time) accepted Imām al-Shādhilī as a passenger, and the Imām boarded with his companions. The famous incident of the wind, the contrary vessel, and the conversion of the Christian captain to Islam took place upon that voyage; and Ḥizb al-Baḥr was inspired into the Imām's heart on the same journey, as he stood between the wind and the wave.
